Katalog Berita (Halaman 31/57)

#5357. Allstate outage: how to file a claim or get roadside help while systems are down

What to do during an Allstate outage, from calling your agent and documenting damage to protecting proof of insurance and avoiding scams that target policyholders

A local Allstate $ALL agent is a human contact who can answer coverage questions, help start a claim and pass details to the company while the app or website is unavailable. Agent contact details usually appear on policy paperwork. That means the office can be reached without logging in to anything.

The declarations page is usually the first place to look. This is the summary sheet that lists a policy's coverages, limits and deductibles, and it often names the servicing agent. Renewal notices, billing statements and welcome letters can carry the same name, phone number and office address.

Older emails, text messages and voicemails from the agency are another record worth checking. A policyholder who saved the agent's number in a phone's contacts already has the quickest route. If an office number turns up through an online search instead, compare it with the printed paperwork before calling.

Policyholders are generally expected to take reasonable steps to stop damage from getting worse, even when they cannot reach their insurer. An app or website being down does not pause that duty. Make temporary fixes, keep every receipt and hold off on permanent repairs until an adjuster has seen the loss.

Standard homeowners policy language spells this out. The common forms published by the Insurance Services Office, which many insurers adapt, list protecting property from further damage among a policyholder's duties after a loss. The same section asks the policyholder to make reasonable and necessary repairs to protect the property. It also asks them to keep an accurate record of what those repairs cost. Individual policies vary, and the wording in your own contract is the one that governs.

A paper or saved copy of your auto insurance ID card lets you prove coverage when Allstate $ALL's app or website won't load. Keep one printed card in the vehicle and one image stored directly on your phone. That way, your proof of insurance does not depend on a live connection.

Drivers in nearly every U.S. state must carry liability coverage. Police can ask to see proof of it during a traffic stop. Drivers involved in a crash typically exchange insurance details at the scene. A registration renewal or a trip to a motor vehicle office can also call for current proof of coverage.

Many drivers now open their ID card inside an insurer's mobile app instead of carrying paper. That method works only when the app can log in and reach the company's servers. If those systems are unavailable, the card may not display at the moment you need it.

Report a loss to Allstate $ALL as soon as you can, even if the app or website is down. Most insurance policies require prompt notice of a claim, and an outage does not pause that duty. A dated record of each attempt to report shows you acted in good faith.

The requirement usually sits in a section of the policy with a title such as "what you must do after a loss" or "duties after loss." Wording varies, but phrases such as "promptly" or "as soon as practicable" are common. Those terms rarely name a fixed number of days. How quickly you must act depends on the policy language and the law in your state.

Read that section before assuming you have time. Some policies set separate, firmer deadlines for specific steps. A homeowners policy may require a signed, sworn proof of loss within a set period after the insurer asks for one. Many policies also include a clause limiting how long you have to sue the insurer over a disputed claim. State law can also affect these windows. Check both the policy text and your state's rules.

Scammers watch for service disruptions and pose as insurance staff to collect payment details, policy numbers or login credentials. During an Allstate $ALL outage, use only phone numbers and web addresses printed on your policy documents or listed on the company's official website. Never give payment information to someone who contacts you first.

An outage hands fraudsters a ready-made story. Policyholders may already expect something to be wrong with their account. A message claiming that a payment failed or a claim stalled can seem plausible as a result.

The pretexts tend to follow a few patterns. A caller may claim to be a claims representative who needs a bank account number to release a payment. A text message may say coverage will lapse unless a premium is "verified" through a link. An email may ask the recipient to log in again on a page that imitates the insurer's site. Each one pushes for quick action and asks for something sensitive.

An insurance policy is a contract, and a contract does not pause because a login page stops loading. When an insurer's app or website goes dark, that alone does not end the coverage a policyholder has paid for. The same goes for the duties the policy places on the customer, from reporting a loss to keeping coverage paid up.

Much of the routine business of insurance has moved to screens. Drivers pull up digital ID cards at traffic stops. Homeowners upload photos of damage, and premiums get paid with a few taps. That convenience can obscure how much still runs through older channels. Claims can be reported by phone. Agents keep offices and phone lines. Premium payments may be possible through an agent or by mail. Complaints can go to a state regulator that sits entirely outside the insurer's systems.

This guide covers what Allstate $ALL policyholders can do during an Allstate outage or any period when the company's digital tools are unavailable.

The most direct way to report a claim when Allstate $ALL's app or website is unavailable is by phone. Use the claims number printed on your insurance ID card or policy documents. A phone report does not depend on the insurer's digital tools.

Start with the paperwork you already have. Auto insurance ID cards typically list a claims contact. Policy packets, declarations pages, renewal notices and billing statements often carry contact details as well. Saved emails from the insurer may include the number too.

Paper records matter here. A policy folder in a desk drawer still works when screens and logins do not.

Gather your information before you dial. The representative will need your policy number to locate your coverage. Have it written down rather than stored only in an app you cannot open.

The basic facts of the loss come next. These include the date and approximate time, the exact location and a plain description of what happened. List what was damaged and whether anyone was hurt.

Auto claims call for more detail about the other parties. Write down the other driver's name, phone number, insurance company and policy number. Add their license plate and the make and model of their vehicle. If police responded, ask for the report number and keep it with your notes. Names and phone numbers of any witnesses belong in the same place.

Home and property claims need a different set of facts. Note the cause if you know it, such as a storm, a burst pipe, a fire or a break-in. Say whether the home is still safe to live in. For a theft, have the police report number ready.

Stick to what you know during the call. If a detail is uncertain, say so instead of guessing. You can add information as the claim moves forward.

Keep a written record of the conversation. Note the date and time of the call and the name of the representative. Ask for a claim or reference number and write it down before hanging up.

Ask what happens next. Find out when an adjuster is expected to contact you. Ask how to send photos and documents if the online portal cannot accept them.

An agent can do several useful things during a disruption. Agency staff can explain what a policy covers and what the deductible is. They can confirm whether a policy is active and help report a new loss. They can also describe the payment methods the office accepts.

There are limits to that role. Claims are typically investigated and settled by adjusters, not by the selling agent. An agent cannot promise a payout, rewrite policy terms or waive a deadline written into the contract. The agency may also depend on the same company systems that are down. Some lookups or document requests may have to wait until those systems return.

Visiting the office in person can help when phone lines are busy. Bring the policy number, a copy of the insurance ID card and any photos of damage. A short written timeline of what happened and when also helps. Ask the staff member to note the visit in the account file.

Write down the name of each person spoken to at the agency, along with the date and time of the conversation. Agency hours vary from office to office. An office may be closed when a loss happens. Outside those hours, the claims number printed on policy documents remains the main route.

Before any cleanup begins, photograph and film all damage to your home, vehicle or belongings. A visual record made right away shows an adjuster the loss as it first looked. It also does not depend on an insurer's app or website being available.

Start wide. Take shots of the whole room, the full exterior wall or all four sides of the car. These show how far the damage extends. Then move in close on each problem area, such as a cracked windshield, a water stain on drywall or a dented door panel.

A slow video walkthrough can capture detail that still photos miss. Narrate as you film. Name the room, the item and what happened. That ties each clip to a specific part of the claim later.

Most smartphones save the date and time in each photo's file data. Keep the original files rather than edited or cropped versions. Back them up to a computer, a cloud account or an email to yourself. That way the record survives if the phone is lost or damaged.

After a car accident, document the scene as well as the vehicles. Useful images include the positions of the cars, road conditions, traffic signs, the other driver's license plate and any visible injuries. Write down the other driver's name, insurer and policy number. Add contact details for any witnesses. If police respond, note the officer's name and the report number.

For damage at home, build a written list of affected items as you photograph them. Include a description, the approximate age and the brand or model where known. Note where in the home each item was. Receipts, bank or card statements, product manuals and older photos of the items can help support their value.

Where it is safe, keep damaged items until an adjuster has inspected them or said they can go. Discarding a ruined appliance or a soaked rug too early can leave a claim with less proof. Spoiled food and anything that poses a health risk may need to go sooner. Photograph those items before disposal.

Store every photo, video and note in a single folder. When the app or claims website works again, or when you reach a representative by phone, the evidence is ready to share.

The duty has a practical side. Many homeowners policies exclude loss caused by neglect, meaning a failure to use all reasonable means to save and preserve property at and after a loss. A small roof leak left open for days can spread to drywall, flooring and insulation. An insurer may then treat that later damage as preventable.

Typical temporary measures are modest. They include covering a damaged roof with a tarp, boarding up a broken window or shutting off the main water valve after a burst pipe. Moving furniture and electronics away from standing water also counts. So does running fans or a dehumidifier to start drying out a wet room.

For a vehicle, the same logic applies on a smaller scale. Standard personal auto policies carry a similar duty to take reasonable steps after a loss to protect the covered vehicle from further loss. Taping plastic sheeting over a shattered window keeps rain out of the interior. Parking a car with a coolant leak or a damaged tire can prevent engine or wheel damage that the original accident did not cause.

Safety comes before any of this. Do not climb onto a wet or storm-damaged roof. Do not walk through standing water near live electrical outlets. For hazardous work, a licensed contractor or emergency water-mitigation company can handle the job instead.

Keep the line between temporary and permanent work clear. Replacing a whole roof or tearing out cabinets before an adjuster inspects can make the claim harder to verify. Save invoices, receipts and payment records for every emergency purchase, from tarps and plywood to a contractor's call-out fee. Note the date of each step as well. A clear timeline is easier to present once the claim is reported.

If damage forces you out of your home, save every receipt for the extra costs of living somewhere else. Additional living expense coverage, often called loss of use, may reimburse those costs. It pays only if your policy includes it, and usually only for spending above your normal budget.

This coverage is common in homeowners and renters policies. Standard homeowners forms usually list it as Coverage D, loss of use. Your declarations page shows whether you have it and what limit applies. Read that page before assuming any expense will be paid.

The coverage typically applies when a covered loss, such as a fire or a burst pipe, makes the home unfit to live in. A loss the policy excludes generally won't trigger it. Flood damage under a standard homeowners policy is one example.

Reimbursement is generally based on the increase in your costs, not the full amount you spend. Mortgage or rent payments usually continue after a loss. A hotel bill on top of them is typically an added cost. Meals work differently. If your household normally spends a set amount on groceries, the claim usually covers the difference between that and what you now spend eating out.

That makes proof of your normal spending useful. Bank statements or past grocery receipts can show your typical monthly costs before the loss.

Keep receipts for hotel stays or short-term rentals, restaurant meals, laundry services and pet boarding. Save records of extra fuel or mileage if a temporary address lengthens your commute. Storage unit fees and the cost of moving into temporary housing also belong in the file.

Photograph each paper receipt as soon as you get it. Thermal receipt paper fades over time. Store the images in email or a cloud folder that doesn't depend on the insurer's app or website. A simple log with the date, amount, vendor and reason for each expense makes the claim easier to review.

Auto policies handle this separately. Rental reimbursement coverage is an optional add-on that may pay for a rental car while a covered vehicle is being repaired. If your auto declarations page doesn't list it, rental costs are generally your own.

Before committing to a large or long-term expense, such as a monthly lease, confirm with your agent or adjuster that it falls within your coverage. A written approval, even a short email, gives you a record to point to if the expense is questioned later.

A screenshot avoids that problem. Save the image to the phone's photo library or files folder. From there, it opens without an internet connection. A PDF downloaded from an online account works the same way. Zoom $ZM in on the saved copy to confirm that the policy number and dates are readable.

A printed card serves as the backup to the backup. Phones run out of battery, crack and get left at home. A paper card in the glovebox stays with the car no matter who is driving it. ID cards usually list the specific vehicle they cover. Households with more than one insured vehicle need a card for each car.

Insurance ID cards show effective and expiration dates. A card from an earlier policy term does not prove current coverage. Replace printed and saved copies each time the policy renews or a vehicle is added or removed.

Save the declarations page as well. It lists the coverages, limits, deductibles, drivers and vehicles on the policy. A stored PDF of it puts the policy details within reach when you report a claim or answer questions from another driver's insurer.

Rules on whether police and motor vehicle agencies accept electronic proof of insurance differ from state to state. A paper copy covers situations where a digital image is not accepted. Your state's motor vehicle agency can confirm the rules that apply where you drive.

If an outage stops you from paying a premium online, write down every attempt and keep proof of it. Then read your policy's grace period and cancellation language. Those terms, not the status of an app or website, decide what happens to a late payment.

A useful record is simple. Note the date and time of each try, the payment method you used and what happened. If a payment page shows an error message, take a screenshot that captures the date and time on your device. If a payment goes through by any route, save the confirmation number, receipt email or bank reference.

Check your bank or card statement before trying again. A payment that appeared to fail may still have been processed. A second attempt could then produce a duplicate charge. Policyholders enrolled in automatic payments should confirm that the scheduled withdrawal left their account on the expected date.

A local Allstate $ALL agent's office may be able to accept a payment or explain other options while the online portal is down. Billing statements and policy paperwork generally list a mailing address for checks. If you mail a payment, use a service that documents the mailing date, such as certified mail through the U.S. Postal Service. Keep a copy of the check and the mailing receipt.

Grace period terms vary by policy, by type of coverage and by state. Some policies allow a window after the due date, and its length is not uniform. Do not assume one applies to your policy or matches the terms of an earlier policy. The billing and cancellation sections of the policy, along with any billing notice, set out the actual rules.

State insurance laws generally require an insurer to send written notice before canceling a policy for nonpayment. The notice rules, including how far in advance it must arrive, differ from state to state. A cancellation notice typically names a date by which payment must be received to keep coverage in force. Read any such notice closely if one arrives during or after a service disruption.

A lapse can carry consequences beyond the policy itself. Most states require drivers to carry auto liability insurance, and a gap in coverage can trigger state penalties. Mortgage lenders and auto lenders often require continuous coverage. If a borrower's policy lapses, a lender may buy coverage on the borrower's behalf, usually at a higher cost.

The payment log matters if a billing dispute arises later. Dated records of on-time attempts through more than one channel give a policyholder something concrete to show the insurer.

Late notice can put a claim at risk. Courts in many states apply what is known as the notice-prejudice rule. Under it, an insurer generally must show that a delay harmed its ability to investigate before denying a claim for lateness. Not every state follows that rule, and it may not cover every type of policy. Reporting early keeps the question from arising.

If digital channels fail, use another route and document it. Write down the date, time, method and outcome of every attempt, including calls that went unanswered. Save screenshots of error messages showing the app or site was unavailable. These records help show that the delay did not start with you.

Written notice adds a second layer of proof. An email to your agent carries its own timestamp, and a dated letter serves the same purpose. Include your policy number, the date and location of the loss and a short description. Sending a letter by USPS Certified Mail with a return receipt gives you proof of delivery.

Some losses carry reporting duties outside the insurer. Auto policies commonly require you to notify police after a vehicle theft. Uninsured motorist coverage for a hit-and-run often requires a police report as well. File those reports promptly, and keep each report number with your claim records.

If Allstate $ALL does not respond to a claim, a payment problem or a coverage question within a reasonable time, a policyholder can file a complaint with their state's insurance regulator. Every state runs an office that accepts consumer complaints about insurers.

Insurance in the U.S. is regulated mainly at the state level rather than by a single federal agency. Congress affirmed that arrangement in the McCarran-Ferguson Act, passed in 1945. The agency that oversees an Allstate policy therefore depends on the state where the policy was issued. The location of the company's headquarters does not decide it.

The office goes by different names. Many states call it the department of insurance. Others use a division of insurance or an insurance commissioner's office. In New York, insurance oversight sits with the Department of Financial Services. The National Association of Insurance Commissioners keeps a directory of state regulators on its website. The official state government site will also list the correct agency.

A complaint makes the most sense after direct contact has failed. That means the policyholder has already tried the claims line, the local agent or written correspondence. It also means they have not received an answer or a fair resolution. Regulators generally expect consumers to give the insurer a chance to fix the problem first.

A useful complaint is specific. It should include the policy number and the claim number, if one exists. It should also name anyone the policyholder spoke with and give a timeline of each contact attempt. Copies of letters, emails, photos and receipts help a reviewer see what happened. A clear statement of the outcome the policyholder wants also helps the review.

Most state departments accept complaints through an online form. Many also take them by mail or phone. After a complaint arrives, the department typically forwards it to the insurer and asks for a written response. A reviewer then checks whether the company followed the policy terms and state law.

A regulator does not act as the policyholder's lawyer. It usually cannot settle a factual dispute over how much a claim is worth. Complaint records still serve a purpose beyond the individual case. State regulators use them to spot patterns in how an insurer treats customers. Recurring problems can lead to a formal market conduct examination of the company.

Caller ID offers little protection. Phone numbers can be spoofed to display a legitimate company name or a familiar area code. Email sender names can be faked the same way. A display name that matches the insurer is not proof the message came from it.

The safer move is to end the contact and start a new one yourself. Hang up or close the message. Then dial the number on your ID card, declarations page or a past bill. A local agent you already work with is another route. If the original request was genuine, someone on that verified line can confirm it.

Links in unexpected texts and emails call for the same caution. Typing the insurer's address directly into a browser avoids lookalike domains that differ by a single letter or an added word. Passwords and one-time security codes should never go to anyone who calls or writes asking for them.

Suspected scams can be reported. The Federal Trade Commission collects fraud reports from consumers. The National Insurance Crime Bureau accepts tips about insurance fraud. Many state insurance departments also run fraud units that take reports of people impersonating insurers.

Anyone who already shared card or bank details should contact the bank or card issuer right away to flag the account. Keep a copy of the suspicious message, along with the number or address it came from.

#5356. Uncommon Thinkers: Saf Rabah wants to make it easier to build housing, one permit at a time

by Grace Kaste on Nov 24, 2026 at 9:50 amNovember 24, 2026 at 1:22 pm

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

When startup founder Safouen (Saf) Rabah decided to get in on the AI boom, he didn’t start by coding or by training any models. He got in touch with urban planners at Bellevue City Hall, and together they combed through nearly 300 land use permit applications to find common mistakes and bottlenecks.

Bellevue began using Rabah’s platform, Govstream.AI, in the summer of 2025, starting with an AI assistant for city staff. In a test using past applications, about three times as many were judged complete with Govstream’s tool. Rabah says that change alone has the potential to alter the housing stock of the city.

“Why can’t we build more housing? All the macro economic reasons, inflation, material costs, labor, land scarcity, are all exacerbated by the slow permitting process,” Rabah said. “That’s what we want to change.”

So, how did Rabah, a B2B software engineer by training, find his way to land use permitting?

Rabah hadn’t heard of the government technology sector, aka GovTech, until mid-career, but looking back, the signs were all there. He was born in Sfax, Tunisia, and grew up in Tunis. Throughout his childhood, he dreamed of running for office.

“I come from a small developing country, so there’s always this idea of, what could a small developing country become? How can it prosper and grow?” Rabah said. “Building has always been a big part of what I imagined myself doing.”

As a teenager in the 1980s, he attended a USAID-funded boarding school in Tunis. The school was part of Cold War efforts to expand American soft power around the Middle East; classes were conducted in English and many of the students went on to university in North America.

“The school had the first Macintosh lab in all of Africa,” Rabah said. “I can still picture the USAID logo on the back of each computer.”

Rabah got a scholarship to University of British Columbia, where he studied electrical engineering while running what he calls his “first entrepreneurial venture”: a service that built and hosted websites for small businesses.

That led to a job at a startup called Pivotal, a customer relationship management platform where Rabah led a team responsible for e-business applications. After Pivotal went public, Rabah left for a job at TELUS, one of Canada’s “big three” telecommunications corporations, but quickly felt frustrated by the dynamics at such a large company.

“Even though I worked on nascent products, it was very, very bureaucratic,” Rabah said. “There were committees, a hundred thousand employees. I missed building things.”

Rabah began to look for a new job that would not only allow him to build but also to make a difference.

“Being an immigrant, it’s always tempting to stay content with having a good job, good status,” Rabah said. “But I’ve always enjoyed the ‘what if?’ mindset, the clean slate. It’s this way today, but could we imagine it to be something different?”

That vision led him to Socrata, which in 2010 was just a nascent government technology startup.

“I really connected with the founder,” Rabah said. “It had a really cool mission, it combined the ‘do-well’ with ‘do-good.’”

Socrata was one of the first platforms to host data portals for local governments and federal agencies, allowing citizens to access and map public data sets. Many U.S. cities, including Seattle, still use Socrata’s software today to publish information including crime logs, permits, and budgets.

“We were a big part of pioneering the open data movement,” Rabah said. “At one point almost every major city was our customer, and half the states.”

Socrata was acquired by Tyler Technologies in 2018, and Rabah stayed on until 2024.

“The funny part is today we use that data quite a lot in our work because one of the most popular data sets that any city publishes is its permit data,” Rabah said. “We’ve even built a connector between Socrata and Govstream.”

But once Socrata was acquired, Rabah began to feel the same way he had at TELUS: boxed in by bureaucracy.

“Tyler was a really good company, but it is a big company,” Rabah said. “Tech was getting repetitive, and I was thinking about leaving it altogether.”

“The thing that pushed me over the edge is that AI happened,” Rabah said. “It was one of those moments where once you start working with it, you really can’t help but think, ‘I can revisit virtually every assumption I’ve made over the last 20 years, every constraint.’”

Immediately, he thought of his passion for building—building a startup, building a better country, and literally building a building.

“I’ve been fascinated by the built environment since my Lego days: What makes some cities livable and others not?” Rabah said. “Then, living in Seattle, you see the lack of housing, affordability, and the homelessness problem we have, and you’re like, why can’t we build more housing? I started believing that these problems are in fact solvable if we simply speed things up and simplify things with AI.”

In July of 2024, Rabah began working with his “design partner,” Bellevue’s Development Services Department, to learn more about common permitting problems.

“We started with something visionary and high-level, but you can only get there if you understand the granular problems of the day-to-day,” Rabah said. “So we talked with developers and builders and we talked with the people on the other side of the counter who are processing these permits and guiding these builders.”

He learned that most permitting mistakes are avoidable, like applying for the wrong zone or forgetting to include a north arrow on an architectural plan. Those oversights can send an application back to square one while clogging up the permitting process for all other projects.

“The wait time disproportionately affects lower margin projects,” Rabah said. “It really constrains the supply of housing, especially the housing we need more of, which is the more affordable kind.”

“I’ve always enjoyed the ‘what if?’ mindset, the clean slate. It’s this way today, but could we imagine it to be something different?”

Govstream’s AI assistants are designed to help first-time builders avoid those errors and make permitting faster for everyone. Rabah and his team began by building what they call an “intelligent intake” platform for a city permitting portal, which guided users through preparing to submit their applications.

When Bellevue first tested Govstream’s intake tool on 276 past residential building permit applications, the city reported a completeness rate of 67%, compared with 22% when those applications were originally filed. According to the company, the latest testing has yielded an 88% completeness rate.

More recently, they’ve begun to build out an AI assistant for the backend, which assists city permit techs with the initial review and reduces what Rabah calls “toil,” like answering unnecessary pre-application emails and tracking down missing documents.

Bellevue staff estimated that Govstream’s tools saved them 152 hours over one month this summer by helping them research and respond to pre-application inquiries.

“For a developer, time is money, so the type of housing that can be built in Bellevue will become more affordable,” said Jake Hesselgesser, Bellevue’s development services director. “This technology has a direct and material impact on the cost of housing.”

Eventually, Govstream.AI will be an end-to-end service, assisting in later stages of the permitting process, too. But Rabah is emphatic that Govstream will not give AI the final say.

“We always put our AI systems in the role of assistants that suggest stuff, but never decide stuff,” Rabah said.

Rabah says Govstream uses preset rules, outside the AI model, to check whether a portion of the application is complete, whether a site needs a geotechnical report, or whether an architect is properly licensed. In Bellevue, city staff retain final authority.

Hesselgesser said that Rabah’s conservative approach to AI is what made the city of Bellevue want to work with his startup.

“Our core principle around Bellevue’s use of AI is to retain human decision making, and we wanted to ensure that we were aligned with a company with the same core value,” Hesselgesser said. “Saf took that holistic approach.”

Around the office, Rabah has become known for his eagerness to build. According to Mariia Derevianko, head of marketing, he spends his weekends building out a product or an idea in order to workshop it with the team.

“He’s very hands-on with the product, with design, marketing, all of the aspects,” Derevianko said. “He never waits for the engineers to build something.”

Most recently, he built a lead tracker to research which cities Govstream should partner with, and previously, he vibe-coded one of the research assistants in the Govstream platform as a template for his software engineers.

Derevianko, who joined the team last year after Rabah poached her from AWS, said he’s also known for his kindness.

“I originally didn’t want to join a start-up,” Derevianko said. “I only said yes because I saw he is a genuinely good person who really cares about this project.”

Govstream.AI has already won at least 12 contracts around the Puget Sound, including King County and the City of Everett, as well as cities across the country, such as Louisville, Kentucky.

Ultimately, Rabah has his eyes set on Seattle, where construction and development has been on the decline. Last December, the city council passed permanent “middle housing” rules to upzone residential neighborhoods and encourage the construction of ADUs, all of which will need a permit.

Seattle tested a competing AI tool from CivCheck in 2025. In June, city staff recommended a pilot that would let applicants check their submissions for completeness before filing.

“We need affordable housing in Seattle,” Rabah said. “We would really, really love to help our home city streamline permitting and remove it as a barrier.”

In founding Govstream.AI, Rabah has found the job he has been looking for: one in which he can build things without the bureaucracy of a large company, all while “doing good.”

“This has become my obsession,” Rabah said. “I can point to things in a city and say, maybe Govstream was a part of what allowed this project to get built.”

#5355. In 2026, many employers are ditching merit-based pay bumps in favor of ‘peanut butter raises’

Professionals have long been taught a simple formula for career success: work hard, outperform your peers, and bigger paychecks will follow. But this year, employers are planning to reward their star staffers differently; instead of factoring in merit, more companies are considering general pay hikes spread out evenly, dubbed the “peanut butter raises” trend.

Around 44% of employers plan to roll out uniform, across-the-board wage bumps in 2026, according to a 2026 Payscale report. About 16% of organizations are newly implementing these “peanut butter” raises: 9% say they already employ the pay strategy, and another 18% of organizations are considering it this year. And top-performing companies are all-in on the approach. Around 56% of organizations that reported that they would exceed their revenue goals in 2025 are using or actively considering peanut butter pay increases.

Companies are still planning to boost employee pay by 3.5%, the same rate as last year. And while 48% of businesses will continue the tradition of awarding pay bumps based on worker performance—which the report described as a “best practice”—the new compensation fad may be trying to alleviate financial headwinds for low-paid workers.

“Tying merit pay increases to performance ratings has come under criticism in recent years for being too subjective and prone to bias,” the Payscale report noted. “At the same time, some organizations have made headlines by electing to standardize pay increases to alleviate administrative burden and reward workers equally, especially for low wage workers where inflation is a big concern.”

Job seekers and staffers alike are suffering through a difficult labor market: Hiring has slowed, layoffs are steadily streaming in, and wages don’t feel like they’re holding up. Looking at the year ahead, the picture doesn’t look too pretty.

Wall Street analysts and business executives have been floating the idea we’re in a “K-shaped economy”; higher-income Americans are witnessing their earnings and wealth rise, while lower-income people are struggling against smaller gains and the high cost of living. The concept has come to explain the confusing U.S. economy, where solid overall growth contrasts with sluggish hiring and rising unemployment.

While U.S. companies are holding their average salary increase budget steady at 3.5%, according to a 2025 report from Willis Towers Watson, there’s a large cohort that is planning to scale back. Nearly a third of businesses plan to lower their compensation-increase budgets compared to last year, citing a potential recession, dwindling financial performance, and desire for more control over costs.

Last year, one high-profile employer ditched its merit-based raises in favor of a general, flat pay bump. Starbucks announced it would be giving a standard 2% raise to all salaried North American employees in 2025, diverging from the norm that managers have a say in the raises of their direct reports. It was all a part of CEO Brian Niccol’s bid to reduce costs in a broader company turnaround effort.

But Starbucks is just one notable name in a growing list of employers hunkering down for economic hardship. Lexi Clarke, Payscale’s chief people officer, told Fortune last year that pay-increase budgets are being slimmed as tariffs and economic woes create uncertainty, forcing many employers to be on their guard.

“Economic concerns have now overtaken labor competition as the primary driver of compensation decisions,” Clarke said, as “66% of employers cite this as the reason for pulling back, up 17% from last year.”

As more companies trim back wage budgets and hand out peanut butter raises, there are many still reinvesting in their star talent. America’s largest private employer, $988 billion retail titan Walmart, unrolled a strategy in 2024 to pay its top store managers up to $620,000 per year.

U.S. CEO John Furner said it was a way to “make managers feel like owners,” acknowledging their success with a slice of the profit pie. Their average base pay was hiked from $130,000 to $160,000, raising their total compensation to between $420,000 and $620,000 annually.

And with more than 4,000 store managers across the U.S. (and around 1.5 million workers) when the policy went into effect, the payout wasn’t just generous—it was a calculated bet on culture.

A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on February 2, 2026.

Emma has also written for publications including the Observer and The China Project, publishing long-form stories on culture, entertainment, and geopolitics. #5354. I have a front-row seat to Norway’s cutting-edge AI newsroom experiment. Even with AI on more than 200 stories a day, a human still checks every one

Christoph Trattner is a professor of information science at the University of Bergen and the founding director of SFI MediaFutures, a research center for responsible media technology. Schibsted Media and Bergens Tidende are partners in the center and help fund it, and he is preparing a funding application with Fjell-Ljom.

Every day, Norway’s largest newspaper, VG, asks an AI model to suggest a headline, search terms and other details for each of its roughly 200 new articles. Before a journalist sees anything, a second model checks the first. In October, across all the newsrooms that use the system, it rejected about one in six of the first model’s attempts. Then the journalist checks the suggestion, and so does an editor, depending on how the newsroom is set up. The cheapest checker goes first, and the people who answer for the story still go last.

“Keep a human in the loop” has become the standard answer to AI’s mistakes. I wanted to know what that human costs, so I asked three Norwegian news organizations what it takes, and whether that has gone up or down as the tools improved. What I learned is that the cost of a check depends heavily on who does it, and on how close that person is to the original work.

I direct a research center on media technology in Norway, where newsrooms began publishing AI-written summaries in 2023. The answers come from the AI Foundations unit at Schibsted Media, the group that owns VG and the regional daily Bergens Tidende; from an editor at Bergens Tidende; and from an editor at Fjell-Ljom, a small local paper in the mountain town of Røros. I am not a neutral observer here: Schibsted Media and Bergens Tidende are partners in my center and help fund it, and I am preparing a grant application with Fjell-Ljom.

Nobody had a measured figure, and the numbers that exist elsewhere come from surveys, not stopwatches. But in one newsroom I could set the check against the work it replaces.

At Bergens Tidende, known as BT, reporters publish 15 to 20 stories of their own a day. AI is not, for now, permitted to write them, but it does write a short version of the finished story, which the reporter is responsible for checking before an editor checks it too. Jan Stian Vold, BT’s development editor, estimates that a reporter who knows the story needs anything from a few seconds to a couple of minutes, and that the editor’s look adds a minute or two. Writing the short version by hand, he told me, takes a reporter three to five minutes. These are his estimates, not measurements. Still, for the person who wrote the story, checking the machine’s version takes less time than writing one.

Vold’s guess is that about one short version in ten needs a fix, and he says the summaries have kept improving with the models. The usual problem is clumsy grammar, or a summary that misses what the reporter considers the most important point. “Almost never hallucinations,” he wrote to me. As far as BT knows, it has never published a critical mistake this way.

Office workers describe something different. In a Workday survey of 3,200 employees who use AI at large companies, nearly 40% of the time AI saved was lost to rework. In a survey of 1,150 U.S. employees by researchers at BetterUp and Stanford, each piece of workslop, AI-generated work that looks finished and is not, took nearly two hours to deal with. These are self-reports about longer documents, not a like-for-like comparison with a newsroom summary. But one difference stands out. In the office, the check often falls to someone who did not do the work and first has to find out what a right answer would look like. At BT, it falls to the one person who already knows.

A Georgia Tech researcher argued this month that catching AI’s mistakes is a mental burden that eats the gains. In the one newsroom where I could estimate it, the check took less time than the writing it replaced, and the reason is who does the checking.

Johanna Johansson, who works in AI Foundations at Schibsted Media, told me that “hallucinations are surprisingly common.” Vold had written “almost never.” Both can be right. She was speaking of AI-generated content in general, he of one narrow task, the summary of a text the reporter has just finished. Two things may be at work here, and I cannot separate them: a narrow task may produce fewer errors, and a checker who knows the material may spot the ones that remain faster.

On one point they agree. “Generally we always have a human in the loop,” Johansson said. That was always a firm principle, she said, and the huge improvements in the models have not made it any less important.

A judgment call, I would add, is the kind of error that only someone who knows the story is likely to notice.

So has the checking gone up or down? For BT’s newsroom as a whole, Vold could not say. His own work is administration and presentations, not journalism, and there his checking has gone down as he has learned to use AI as an assistant and not as a source of facts. At Fjell-Ljom it has stayed constant, because it was never a separate step. What nobody described is letting go of the check on what gets published.

I think they are right to hold that line, and the reason goes beyond the errors that remain. The check at BT is cheap because of everything the reporter did before the summary appeared. Hand the same summary to someone who had not reported the story, and the check would either take far longer or turn into a formality. A freelance journalist interviewed for a 2025 master’s thesis at Aalto University made a similar point: typing out an interview word for word “really gets you inside it in a way that reading over a transcription and just checking for errors doesn’t.”

For companies outside the news business, I take three things from this. Count the check: how many items, how many people look at each one, and how many minutes each look takes. Then set that against what the task took before. Do not treat a falling error rate as permission to stop checking. Nobody I asked has. Above all, give the check to the person who knows the work, instead of adding a reviewer downstream who has to start from nothing. In these newsrooms, that is what keeps the check manageable.

As AI takes over more of what comes before the check, I would worry less about the minutes than about whether anyone is left who can tell in seconds that something is wrong.

AI disclosure: The author drafted this piece with Claude (Anthropic), working from his interview notes and the newsrooms’ emails, and used it to search for and check the published studies cited. The reporting and the argument are his own, and he takes responsibility for the text.

The opinions expressed in Fortune.com commentary pieces are solely the views of their authors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions and beliefs of Fortune.

#5353. Hackers breach Air Force cloud as cyberattacks hit the CIA, FBI and Pentagon

Reuters tracked 2026 intrusions at the Air Force, CIA, FBI, Pentagon and more. Five incidents, and who did it is still unclear.

A government hack is often pictured as one dramatic event, but in 2026 break-ins at U.S. agencies became public one after another. President Trump confirmed in a Fox News interview on Nov. 21 that hackers had broken into an FBI database, according to CNBC, and within days the public learned of a breach at an intelligence agency as well. Each new disclosure arrived before the last one had been explained. The targets also went beyond spy and military agencies to departments that most people rarely connect with national security.

What ties these breaches together is not a single attacker but how little is known about what the intruders took. No one has spelled out exactly what they got at the intelligence agency, according to the Honolulu Star-Advertiser, or which records they removed from the FBI database. Justin Sherman, a senior associate at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, says no database hack should be waved off as routine because each one connects to others, according to TIME. A breach in 2026 is best judged by what the intruders could reach, not by a confirmed count of stolen files.

Reuters lists the major cyber intrusions of 2026 into U.S. government agencies and other targets. Intruders got into the Air Force's main cloud platform and into a research tool that the CIA shares with the country's top intelligence office, while other attackers went after dozens of commercial ships. What each intruder could reach shows where the real exposure lies, from weapons data and intelligence tools to police records, personnel files and shipping.

Hackers who broke into Cloud One, the Air Force's flagship computing platform, got into the part of the system that manages the entire platform rather than a single application. They reached its control plane by exploiting a software flaw, according to TNW. From there, the intruders potentially exposed aircraft and radar data, along with data from a munitions system used at more than 200 sites.

Getting into the controls does not prove that anyone read the data behind them. No one has shown that the intruders looked at any aircraft or parts records, or publicly identified who got in. U.S. Cyber Command is assessing the damage. The Air Force said in a statement to Reuters that it "does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities or operational status of specific networks and systems."

Whether or not the hackers took anything, the Air Force has already lost the use of its flagship cloud for new work. The service's plan to shift its back-office programs onto the platform is on hold, and the software already hosted there can no longer receive updates.

A breach at an intelligence agency makes most people picture stolen secrets, but these hackers got into the tool the agencies use to read the open world. They accessed the open-source scanning system of the CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, which scans unclassified, publicly available material.

The only public reassurance is narrow. The Office of the Director of National Intelligence said there were "no disruptions to critical capabilities or classified systems." That statement rules out breakage, not entry.

Early signs point to possible Chinese involvement, but no account of how the intruders got in has been made public, so China remains a suspicion rather than a confirmed finding.

The hackers reached a tool two intelligence agencies use, and who did it is still unsettled.

At the Defense Manpower Data Center, hackers went after the people who serve and support the military, not its weapons or its intelligence tools. An earlier intrusion into the center affected 2.76 million living people, a fraction of the more than 60 million people the agency held records on in fiscal 2024.

For the people in those files, the risk is personal. The exposed details include birthdates and military specialties, which together link who a person is to the work that person does for the military.

Intruders were inside the center's systems for months before anyone noticed. Unauthorized access began in October 2025, and no one found the weakness that let them in until July 16, 2026. No one has publicly named the attacker.

The people in those files may not learn for years whether anyone has used their details.

At Cloud One, the hackers did harm simply by getting in, and any theft that comes to light would only add to it.

The FBI suffered two breaches in one fall. The first came in September, when intruders took data on FBI employees and forced the agency to shut down part of its operations until the breach was resolved. The second reached the National Crime Information Center, a shared criminal-justice system that police well beyond the FBI rely on, so a breach there becomes a problem for every department that checks a name against it.

This breach puts everyday police records at risk, so what matters is whether departments can still trust what they look up. The September theft was the work of a cybercrime group called ShinyHunters, which shows criminal hackers, not only foreign governments, are getting inside federal law enforcement. No one has publicly named who broke into the criminal database.

When Trump talked about the database break-in, he spoke of a possible upside rather than the damage, suggesting the breach might turn up evidence of voter fraud. "I always like to put things on a positive spin," Trump said.

Police nationwide still rely on a system whose breach the government has acknowledged but not explained.

The 2026 breaches reached civilian departments and commercial ships as well as spy and military systems. Personnel data leaked from the Department of Homeland Security, intruders broke into the Treasury Department, and as many as 50 ships carrying oil and other explosive cargo are believed to have been hit by cyberattacks. No details have been made public on what the intruders reached at either department.

Iran is the primary suspect in the ship attacks, according to The Wall Street Journal, and U.S. officials also see Russia as a possible culprit. A Trump administration official disputed that, saying the U.S. has found no evidence of Iranian involvement and that four attacks amounted to little more than a minor nuisance. Coast Guard cyber teams have responded to at least four of the ships as they approached U.S. ports.

The attackers are exploiting a flaw in Fortinet $FTNT routers that are popular in the maritime industry. Some ships also received bomb threats, and the attacks come as Iran continues to mount physical attacks against ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

The ship attacks can't easily turn a tanker into a weapon, but a hacked vessel can still stall a cargo of fuel.

#5352. Electric boat maker Zin Boats raises $5M and launches propulsion business beyond the water

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 24, 2026 at 9:58 amNovember 24, 2026 at 9:58 am

Zin Boats made a splash with fast, pricey electric boats. But most of its business is now coming from what’s under the floor.

The Seattle startup has launched Zin Power, a new division that will supply its electric propulsion systems to other boat builders and to industries that rely on diesel engines, such as construction and mining.

The company also raised $5 million to scale up production and expanded its headquarters in the Interbay neighborhood to 11,000 square feet.

About 90% of the company’s revenue comes from selling motors and batteries to customers in the marine and drone industries, founder and CEO Piotr Zin told GeekWire. A typical setup includes two motors and about 500 kilowatt-hours of battery storage.

“We noticed a steady demand for pleasure craft year over year, but at the same time a massive increase in propulsion sales,” Zin said.

Customers include StanCraft Wooden Boats, which teamed with Zin on the 340 Hammerhead E, an all-electric wooden runabout. StanCraft delivered the first one to a customer this summer.

GeekWire first checked out the company in early 2024, when it was relaunching after a pandemic shutdown with its Z2R, a 20-foot carbon fiber runabout. Later that year Zin showed off the Z11, a 37-foot electric tender designed to shuttle passengers to and from megayachts at more than 60 mph. The company said boats on the platform would cost $1.75 million to $3.75 million.

The company also offers the Z7 Convertible, a 22-foot runabout with a removable roof that it pitches for fishing, surfing and cruising. The boat has a top speed of 40 mph and a range of more than 80 miles

Zin Power grew out of the drivetrains engineered for those boats. Zin sees the marine track record as a selling point for other industries that need high torque, including construction, mining and remotely operated vehicles (ROVs).

“The ocean is one of the harshest environments there is, so the technology has already proven itself under about the toughest conditions it could face,” Zin said.

Many of those machines still run on diesel engines, a technology more than a century old. Zin said operators are eager to switch to electric.

“What’s interesting is that economics is driving the shift, not regulation or image,” he said.

Electric systems cost up to 70% less to operate, according to Zin. He estimated that replacing a single 250-horsepower industrial diesel engine that runs eight hours a day could save as much as $1.5 million over 10 years.

The new funding will pay for more manufacturing capacity, a dedicated sales and engineering team to work with boat builders, and support for customers converting from diesel. Zin calls it a seed round, with a larger raise planned down the road. The company has raised $6.5 million to date, including a $1.275 million seed round in early 2024.

Zin Boats has nine full-time employees and brings on about a dozen contractors as needed.

For now, each Zin Power system is built to order. The company’s motors range from 100 to 600 kilowatts and deliver up to 2,700 pound-feet of torque, and its systems can run fully electric or as hybrids. A proprietary control unit that Zin Power calls the “Magic Box” manages everything from charging and cooling to software and safety.

“Our goal is to keep delivering what we’ve built while developing simpler, more advanced plug-and-play systems,” Zin said. “Eventually, we want a customer to be able to pull out a diesel engine and drop in a Zin Power system as a direct one-for-one replacement.”

#5351. Chanel’s CEO Leena Nair makes the case for human made ‘beauty and creation.’ In an era of AI saturation, her $19 billion-a-year business depends on it

The chief executive of one of the world’s leading fashion brands has said that the intense and often slow process of craftswomen and men making products by hand has become a vital skill in a world of online “instant gratification.”

Leena Nair, the CEO of Chanel, said that business leaders are living through an “unprecedented” period of transformation and fragility, adding that it was time to prioritize human ingenuity and talent.

“Macro-economic shifts, huge leaps in AI and technology and geopolitical instability, these are challenges affecting all sectors,” she told the annual gala dinner of the French Chamber of Great Britain, which brings together U.K. and French business executives, policy makers, and cultural leaders.

“And in this context of disruption, the power of creation and beauty has never been more vital or more precious. Creation and beauty have been vital sources of inspiration and joy for thousands of years. They’re even more precious today in a world of constant instant gratification, constant overstimulation, and infinite touch points.”

Nair, who has been Chanel CEO since 2022, saw the luxury brand return to growth last year, led by an increase in sales in America. Global revenues rose by 1.8% compared with 2024 to $19.3 billion, while operating profits rose 5.2% to $4.7 billion.

Nair said there was a growing body of scientific evidence that revealed that exposure to art and human-led creative work led to higher levels of happiness and performance.

“This growing body of academic research shows how encounters with beauty correlate directly to a greater sense of human flourishing at work and in life,” she said. “In recent years, we see growing scientific evidence of the improving impact that arts and culture has on physical and mental well-being.”

“In this context of disruption, the power of creation and beauty has never been more vital or more precious”

Over 95% of Chanel’s customers are women, Nair said, adding that “beauty” is a very important driver of how people respond to the world around them. She said that one customer who had been through surgery said that buying crafted products was part of her recovery.

“Surgeons tell me this all the time, that when surgery is over they know the women are back to normal when they ask to put on their makeup for the first time,” she said.

Many leaders of luxury brands often feel ignored when it comes to policy debates about economic growth. In the U.K., the end of foreign visitors being able to shop without incurring the national sales tax has caused controversy. In the U.S., new tariffs targeting luxury goods have unsettled markets.

“Luxury is an economic powerhouse, it’s a cultural powerhouse and an emotional powerhouse,” Nair said. “To put that scale into context, European high-end luxury brands generate a trillion dollars in business every year. That’s 5% of Europe’s GDP. “It’s not a niche sector. More than 2 million people work in the sector across Europe.”

Chanel works with the King’s Foundation, King Charles III’s organization that supports the retention and development of traditional skills.

“It looks simple, but to do a pleated skirt takes eight hours of pushing a cardboard mold back and forth by two talented artisans doing it the right way,” Nair said, arguing that Chanel continues to invest in “skills that will otherwise be lost, working with extraordinary artisans and partners, many of whom we have worked with for generations.”

Kamal Ahmed is the executive editorial director of Europe and the Middle East. Kamal is the author of Letter from London, Fortune Europe's weekly take on global business as seen from London. Previously, he was director of audio at The Telegraph and presenter of The Daily T podcast.

#5350. Buy now, pay later on Black Friday: 7 checks before you split a payment

Using buy now, pay later on Black Friday can make holiday deals easier to manage, but fees, due dates, returns and credit checks deserve a look first

A split payment changes when you pay for something, not what you owe for it. That distinction is easy to lose at checkout, where a pay-in-four button can make a large purchase look like a small one.

Black Friday is the day after U.S. Thanksgiving, which falls on the fourth Thursday of November. It opens a stretch of holiday shopping that runs straight into December bills. Retailers promote deals with short deadlines, and checkout pages often list installment plans alongside cards and digital wallets. Providers such as Klarna, Afterpay, Affirm and PayPal $PYPL appear at checkout on many retail sites, and some stores offer their own versions.

The basic model works like this. A pay-in-four plan divides a purchase into four equal payments. The first is due when you check out. The rest are collected on a set schedule, usually by automatic charge to a linked card. Longer plans stretch payments over months and can carry interest. Each provider writes its own terms, and those terms can change.

That variation is the reason to slow down before using buy now, pay later on Black Friday. Two plans that look identical on a product page can still differ. They may treat missed payments, returns and credit reporting in different ways. The answers sit in the provider's app and disclosures, not in the retailer's banner ad.

The checks below are meant to be done before you tap the button, not after the confirmation email arrives. They start with the total amount you will repay and how it compares with the sticker price. They move through late-fee rules, the timing of each installment against your paydays and the card that will be charged. They also cover how refunds work when an item goes back and how providers handle credit checks and reporting. The last covers how to keep track of several plans running at once.

Each check answers a specific question about a specific plan. The result is a checkout decision made with the full terms in view, rather than one made under the pressure of a sale clock.

Before agreeing to a buy now, pay later plan, compare the total you will repay with the sticker price of the item. If the two figures match, the plan changes only when you pay. If the total is higher, the difference is what the borrowing costs.

On a pay-in-four plan, the four installments together should equal the checkout price. If they add up to more, find out what the extra covers before confirming.

Longer plans can work differently. Monthly installment loans from providers such as Affirm can carry interest. Once interest applies, the payments added together can exceed the price on the tag. At the same rate, a loan that runs longer gives interest more time to build.

Rates differ by provider and by shopper. Two people buying the same television from the same retailer may be offered different terms. A rate seen on a friend's plan, or on an earlier purchase, says little about the offer on the screen today.

The check itself is simple arithmetic. Find the installment amount and the number of payments on the plan summary shown before you confirm. Multiply the installment amount by the number of payments. Then set that figure beside the full checkout price, including tax and shipping. If the multiplied figure is larger, the gap is the price of spreading the cost out.

Check the number of payments as closely as the amount. A plan with a smaller installment may simply run for more months. A lower monthly figure does not mean a lower total.

The comparison carries extra weight on discounted items. Black Friday sales are built around markdowns. Interest charged on a sale item eats into the discount. Depending on the rate and the length of the loan, it can shrink the saving or erase it. The fair comparison is the sale price paid outright, not the original price the retailer crossed out.

When the total repaid exceeds the sticker price, the shopper has a clear choice. One path is to accept that extra cost knowingly. The other is to pay a different way.

Know what a buy now, pay later provider does when an installment is missed before you split a Black Friday purchase. Klarna and Afterpay may charge late fees. Affirm has said it does not charge late fees.

A shopper who picks one of these providers at checkout is also picking the rules for the weeks after the sale. The missed-payment rules come from the provider's agreement with the shopper.

Fee policies can change. A provider can revise its terms. The version that applied to a purchase last year may not match the one in force this Black Friday. The reference that counts is the current agreement shown in the provider's app or disclosures at the time of purchase.

The word "may" in a fee summary matters too. Whether a fee applies to a specific order is set out in the current terms, not in a general description of the provider.

Reading that agreement means looking for a few specific answers. Does the provider charge anything for a missed installment? If it does, is the charge a flat amount or tied to the size of the order? Does the agreement set a limit on total fees for a single purchase?

Timing is the next thing to look for. Check whether the terms describe a window after a missed due date before any fee applies. Check whether the provider tries the charge again, and when. See whether a due date can be moved before it arrives.

A fee is not the only rule worth knowing. Look for what a missed payment means for using the same provider on later orders. The same app may appear at checkout again before the holiday shopping season ends.

Affirm's statement covers late fees only. It does not describe everything else in its agreement. The rest of its terms still need a full read.

A screenshot of the fee section taken at checkout creates a record of the rules shown when you agreed. That record helps if a question about a charge comes up weeks later. Keep it with the order confirmation.

Before splitting a Black Friday purchase, match each installment's due date to the day money actually lands in your account. The first payment comes out at checkout. The rest follow a schedule the provider sets, not one built around your pay cycle.

Many providers collect the remaining three installments about every two weeks. That pattern is common, but it is not universal. Schedules vary by provider. The exact dates appear at checkout and in the provider's app, and those are the dates that count.

On a two-week rhythm, the last payment lands roughly six weeks after the purchase. Black Friday falls in late November. A plan opened that day would run into early January.

That window matters because of what else sits inside it. December brings regular monthly bills, and often more holiday spending on top of them. A split payment taken on Black Friday adds three more draws across the same weeks. Putting them on a calendar before checkout makes the overlap visible.

The practical step is to write down your income dates for the next six weeks. Then place each installment date beside them. If an installment falls a day or two before a paycheck arrives, that payment has to come from money already in the account. If it falls just after payday, it competes with rent, utilities and other fixed costs due around the same time.

The first installment deserves separate attention. It is charged on Black Friday itself, whatever your pay schedule. A shopper paid at the end of the month may be near the bottom of the cycle when that charge hits.

Someone paid every two weeks may find the installments line up closely with paydays. Someone paid once a month may see most installments fall between paychecks. Neither pattern rules out a plan on its own. What matters is knowing which one applies before agreeing to the terms.

Do not assume a due date can be moved later. If a provider offers any way to change one, its terms will spell that out. Read them before relying on that option.

The card linked to a buy now, pay later plan determines what a short balance will cost. A debit card exposes the shopper to bank overdraft or declined-payment fees, while a credit card adds its own interest on any balance carried.

Installments on split-payment plans are usually charged automatically to the card the shopper links at checkout. Each later payment comes off that card on its due date, with no further action needed. The card chosen during a Black Friday checkout shapes what happens on every one of those dates.

A debit card draws directly on a bank account. The money leaves the account on the day the installment is collected, not the day the item was bought. If the balance is short on that day, the bank may cover the charge and apply an overdraft fee. It may instead refuse the charge and apply a declined-payment fee.

Those bank charges sit apart from the BNPL plan itself. A refused charge can also leave the installment unpaid. That brings the provider's own missed-payment rules into play. Reading both the bank's fee terms and the provider's terms covers each side of that risk.

The practical risk with debit funding is timing inside the account. Rent, utilities, subscriptions and other automatic debits may draw on the same balance in the same week. An installment that looked small at checkout can be the charge that pushes the account below zero.

A credit card moves the installments off the bank account, but it does not remove cost. Each installment joins the card's balance. If the shopper carries part of that balance from month to month, the card's interest applies to it.

That means a plan with no interest of its own can still end up costing interest. The card issuer charges that interest, not the BNPL provider. The card also has its own payment date, separate from the installment schedule.

Before confirming a split payment, a shopper can check which card the plan will charge and what that card's terms say about carried balances. For a debit card, the useful question is whether the linked account will hold enough on each collection date, not only on Black Friday itself.

A refund on a buy now, pay later purchase goes through the BNPL provider, not only the retailer. Installments may keep coming due until the return is processed. Read the store's return policy and the provider's refund process before you check out.

A split payment creates two separate relationships. The retailer decides whether an item can come back and how long you have to send it. The provider manages the loan, including how a refund is applied to your plan.

Start with the retailer. Find the return window for the specific item you are buying. Check whether the product page or receipt marks it as final sale or lists different conditions for discounted stock. Black Friday markdowns deserve this extra look before you commit.

Then turn to the provider. Its refund process explains what happens to an installment plan once the retailer accepts a return. Look for it in the provider's app or help pages before you agree to the plan, not after a package is already in transit.

The weak point is the gap between sending an item back and the refund posting. A return has to be shipped, received and processed by the retailer. Until that happens, scheduled payments may still be charged to your linked card. Budget for them as though you had kept the item.

Keep a simple paper trail for every split purchase you might return. That means the order confirmation, any return authorization, the shipping receipt and the tracking number. If a refund stalls, those records show when the item left your hands.

If a refund never arrives, or the retailer and provider give different answers, the next step is the provider's own dispute policy. Rules for disputing BNPL purchases in the U.S. have been subject to regulatory change. Do not assume a specific federal protection covers your purchase. Read the provider's current dispute terms, which set out how to raise a problem and what the provider will review.

Gifts bought on an installment plan need one more check. The plan belongs to the buyer, even if someone else sends the item back. Ask the recipient to tell you when they return it, then watch your plan for the adjustment.

Buy now, pay later providers differ on two credit questions: the type of credit check run at approval and whether the loan is reported to credit bureaus. Check both in the provider's disclosures before splitting a Black Friday purchase. One app's answer does not carry over to another.

The first question is about approval. Some buy now, pay later providers run a soft credit check when a shopper applies. Others run a hard credit check. The provider decides which one applies, and its own terms are the place to confirm it.

The second question is about what happens after approval. Some providers report their installment loans to credit bureaus, and some do not. That choice decides whether a plan appears on a shopper's credit file at all.

The two answers are independent. A provider can handle its approval check one way and its bureau reporting another. Each question needs its own look in the disclosures.

The practical step is to open the provider's app or website before checkout. Find the sections that cover credit checks and credit reporting. A sale-day checkout screen may show only the payment amounts. The credit details may sit somewhere else entirely.

When a retailer offers more than one split-payment option, the comparison can include these two points alongside the payment terms. Noting each provider's approach to checks and reporting keeps the options straight. That record also helps when the same shopper sees different providers at different stores over the holiday weekend.

There is no single answer to whether buy now, pay later hurts credit. The question has to be asked plan by plan. Reading that provider's disclosures is the reliable way to know what a specific plan involves.

If a provider's disclosures leave either question unanswered, that gap is something to weigh before agreeing to split the payment. The same check applies to any store-specific plan offered at checkout during Black Friday sales.

Before adding a new buy now, pay later plan during Black Friday sales, list every plan already running, with its next due date and remaining balance. That single tally shows what you already owe before another installment joins the queue.

Split payments are easy to stack. A shopper can hold plans with Klarna, Afterpay, Affirm and PayPal $PYPL at the same time, plus a store-specific option from a single retailer. Each plan runs on its own autopay date. None of them waits for the others.

That separation makes the total hard to see. Each provider's app shows the plans held with that provider. It does not show a pay-in-four plan opened elsewhere a week earlier. A shopper checking one app sees only part of what is owed.

The tally itself needs only three columns. The first names the provider and the item bought. The second records the next due date. The third records the balance still owed on that plan. A notes app, a spreadsheet or a sheet of paper all work.

Fill it in by opening each provider's app or account in turn. Copy the dates and balances directly from those screens rather than from memory. Include store-specific plans. They are easy to miss because they sit inside a retailer's own checkout or account.

Once the list is complete, add up the third column. That sum is the amount still due across every active plan. Then sort the rows by due date. The sorted list shows which days carry more than one payment and how closely the charges bunch together.

Only then look at the new purchase. Add it as a fresh row, with its own first payment and its own future dates. Compare the new total with the old one. If the new row lands on a date that already holds other payments, that clustering is visible before checkout rather than after.

Keep the list current through the rest of the holiday season. Plans opened over the Black Friday weekend can still be collecting payments well into December. Update a row each time a payment clears, and delete it when the balance reaches zero. A plan that is dropped from the list too early, or never added, leaves the total incomplete.
