#5334. Stop Using AI as an Excuse for Layoffs. Here’s How to Use AI to Retain Talent Instead

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

How to use AI to make your team more capable, not smaller.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

When a company announces layoffs and points to AI, I always want to know what happened first. Did the technology fundamentally change how work gets done, or did leadership already need to reduce costs and AI became a convenient explanation?

There is a meaningful difference. AI can automate tasks, accelerate workflows and change the skills a company needs. But AI does not walk into a boardroom and decide how many people should remain employed. Leaders decide what happens to the capacity the technology creates.

That distinction matters because employees are watching. If every AI announcement is followed by layoffs, people quickly learn that greater efficiency puts their jobs at risk and they have little reason to embrace the tools leadership wants them to use.

There is another way to implement AI. Start by asking how it can make your people more capable.

I learned this lesson long before the current AI boom. When we were building Amazon Web Services, talented engineers were spending too much time provisioning servers, configuring storage and handling infrastructure before they could get to the work they were actually there to do. By removing that friction, we gave developers more capacity to build, experiment and solve customer problems.

I saw the same principle years later with a junior attorney who spent hours researching and formatting before reaching the work that required her judgment. Generative AI could produce a first draft in minutes, giving her more time to refine the facts and shape the narrative for the client’s best outcome.

That is the opportunity leaders should look for with AI. Before calculating how many positions an efficiency gain could eliminate, ask what your people could accomplish if repetitive work stopped consuming so much of their day.

Suppose AI gives a team back 10 or 20% of its capacity. What happens to that time?

It could be the customer follow-up that keeps getting postponed, an improvement sitting in the backlog or a relationship that needs more attention. Those opportunities already exist inside most businesses. The problem is that people have been too busy with repetitive work to pursue them.

I saw this with a team of customer service agents who spent a significant portion of their day filling out forms and navigating cumbersome systems. An AI tool automated part of that process and gave them roughly an hour back each day.

Leadership could have used that hour to justify a smaller team. Instead, employees spent more time connecting with customers, strengthening relationships and solving more complex problems. AI removed work they disliked and created room for work where they could contribute more.

Retaining talent requires planning for people at the beginning of an AI initiative rather than after deployment. If leaders automate first and ask what happens to employees later, the priority is already clear.

Before introducing AI, divide the work into three categories. Some tasks contain little meaningful judgment and can be automated. Others can be accelerated by AI while still requiring human judgment. A third group should remain primarily human because relationships, creativity or judgment create the value. Then make the next decision before deploying anything. Where will the recovered capacity go?

That could mean moving people toward customer relationships, product development, higher-level analysis or other work that contributes more directly to growth. The destination will vary by organization, but leaders should know where they want people to go before technology begins changing their roles.

How you introduce AI also shapes whether employees embrace or resist it. If the first message people hear is that a tool will save 40% of their time, they may immediately wonder what leadership plans to do with that 40%.

Tell employees which frustrating work you want to reduce. Show them what they will have more time to accomplish. Explain how their roles can become more valuable as AI handles repetitive tasks.

Then demonstrate that commitment through what happens next. If employees see recovered time consistently reinvested into better work, stronger skills and new opportunities, AI starts to look like a tool they can use rather than a threat they need to survive.

Leaders can begin before buying another AI tool. Take one team and map how AI could change its work, then answer these four questions together before deployment.

1. What work should disappear? Break roles into individual tasks and identify repetitive work that consumes time without requiring significant human judgment. Focus first on removing friction rather than removing positions.

2. What human capability should grow? For every task AI can automate or accelerate, identify what employees could do with the recovered time. Look for work involving customers, relationships, creativity, problem-solving or judgment.

3. Where will the recovered capacity go? Give those hours a destination before deployment. If AI saves a team eight hours each week, decide whether those hours will go toward customer service, innovation, new revenue opportunities or another measurable priority.

4. What will you tell employees? Explain what AI will take off their plates and what you want them doing more of as a result. Managers should be able to describe that future clearly before asking employees to adopt the technology.

AI will change jobs, and some roles will change significantly as companies redesign how work gets done. But leaders still control a critical decision about what they do with the capacity AI creates.

Before treating efficiency as a reason to reduce headcount, ask what your people could accomplish with the time they get back. The companies that answer that question first have an opportunity to use AI for something far more valuable than cutting costs. They can use it to build a more capable workforce.

When a company announces layoffs and points to AI, I always want to know what happened first. Did the technology fundamentally change how work gets done, or did leadership already need to reduce costs and AI became a convenient explanation?

There is a meaningful difference. AI can automate tasks, accelerate workflows and change the skills a company needs. But AI does not walk into a boardroom and decide how many people should remain employed. Leaders decide what happens to the capacity the technology creates.

That distinction matters because employees are watching. If every AI announcement is followed by layoffs, people quickly learn that greater efficiency puts their jobs at risk and they have little reason to embrace the tools leadership wants them to use.

#5333. Crate & Barrel CEO plans a 50-store expansion to win customers from rivals: ‘It’s absolutely a market steal play.’

Few retail CEOs have had a more turbulent run than Janet Hayes. Since taking over Crate & Barrel in 2020, she has steered the furniture retailer through a pandemic and repeated tariff shocks. Now she’s betting the company can come out of it on the offensive.

Hayes hews to the old adage, “Don’t let a good crisis go to waste.” She says she took the tariffs as an opportunity to really understand Crate & Barrel’s supply chain weaknesses and to fix them. On her watch, Crate & Barrel has diversified its supplier base, notably sending more sourcing to Vietnam, and invested in infrastructure and technology to position inventory where it is most likely to sell and better forecast demand. She also moved more upholstery sourcing to the U.S. Crate & Barrel has overhauled everything from its warehouse management software to its e-commerce site. And it now accepts buy-now, pay-later services in an appeal to inflation-pinched consumers.

“You don’t feel it until you’re being tested, but the global supply chain is fragile,” Hayes told Fortune in an interview at the new location of CB2, Crate & Barrel’s sister brand, in New York’s Chelsea district. “You can have the best-laid plans, you can map your ocean liners, you can decide what vendors you’re going to work with, but culture is everything to get through it.”

In her time as CEO, she has worked to flatten decision making at the retailer, to make it more flexible in a furniture market that is, in fact, not growing. “You can get into a command room, but you have to have the people to make it happen,” Hayes says.

Crate & Barrel is part of privately held German retail group Otto Group, which does not publish financial results but did report earlier this year that Crate & Barrel revenue rose 1.6% last year. Given that the furniture market is stagnant in the U.S., Hayes says growth has to come at the expense of the competition. “It’s absolutely a market steal play,” says Hayes, who earlier in her career was a senior executive at Williams-Sonoma and at Nike. Hayes plans on adding 30 new Crate & Barrel and CB2 stores to its current count of 100 in the next three years, as well as 20 more in the two years after that.

As she shows Fortune around the CB2 store, she points to touches that she thinks will help it achieve a more elevated look she sees as key for winning customers from rivals. Things like much bigger rug displays with more swatches and new woods in warmer tones that feel homier. “We are building better quality products,” she says. “You have to bring good quality to the market to be able to do that.”

Phil Wahba is a senior writer at Fortune primarily focused on leadership coverage, with a prior focus on retail.

#5332. Etzioni on AI: 18 ways to use AI this Thanksgiving

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 25, 2026 at 8:17 amNovember 25, 2026 at 10:16 am

Here are 18 creative ways to use AI this Thanksgiving. Some save you time in the kitchen or at the airport, and others aim to make the meal more fun. The don’ts at the end could save your turkey, and my very last suggestion is perhaps the best.

Flight delay forecasting. Apps like Flighty (start with free tier) use machine learning to predict whether your flight will leave on time and why it might not.

Cancellation playbook drafted in advance. Have the backup flights and a rebooking script ready ahead of time, so a cancellation means consulting your AI instead of starting from scratch.

Airport pickup routing. Five relatives land at different times at two airports, and AI works out who drives whom. It can even send a polite request on your behalf.

A personal travel agent. Vayo (free, private beta), a new Seattle startup co-founded by my friend Mike Fridgen, connects to your inbox and pulls in your flight, hotel and restaurant confirmations. It keeps an eye on them for price drops and changes.

Oven Tetris. Give it your oven’s size, every dish’s temperature and the serving time. It works backward to a minute-by-minute schedule and flags the conflicts.

Decoding grandma’s recipe card. Photograph the card and have AI modernize it under one rule: it never invents quantities. “A pinch” stays “a pinch.” “un poco” or “ein bissl” may be translated, but not changed.

Reconstructing a lost dish. Several relatives describe a dish a late grandparent made. AI triangulates a recipe, you cook test versions, and the family votes on which one tastes right.

Pairing from the wines on hand. AI picks from bottles you actually own, and those brought over by guests, dish by dish, instead of a generic list. Last-minute fun!

Potluck dispatcher. One AI thread collects RSVPs and dish claims so you don’t end up with four green bean casseroles.

Trivia built from your own family’s facts. ChatGPT can now run it as a playable game, with answer buttons and a running score inside the conversation.

AI-prepped grandparent interview. Feed the AI what you already know and have it draft questions about the gaps. Record it, and afterward AI turns the transcript into a short illustrated booklet that’s in the mail by Christmas.

Angry Uncle rehearsal. Karin Tamerius, a political psychiatrist, built the Angry Uncle Bot, and it still runs in ChatGPT. A coach asks for your issue and your stance. You set the uncle’s temper from Annoyed to Apoplectic and choose whether he’s drunk or sober, and the coach critiques each reply before he answers.

Live interpreter for multilingual families. Put ChatGPT’s voice mode (paid plans) in the middle of the table so the great-aunt who only speaks Hebrew or Spanish is part of the conversation instead of watching it.

Friday leftover remix. Photograph the fridge and get a menu that makes Friday’s leftovers feel like a new meal.

Specific thank-you notes. Each note names what that person actually brought or said.

Photo triage. AI picks the best 20 of 400 photos and captions them in the family’s inside-joke voice.

“We missed you” letter for someone who wasn’t at the table. AI drafts it from the stories told at dinner.

Black Friday skeptic. Before you buy, check Google’s price insights, which tells you whether a price is high, low or typical for the past three months. Last year, 36% of Black Friday items showed no savings over their prices a few weeks earlier. Better yet, set a price track and let Google’s agent buy the item at eligible U.S. stores when it hits your number, after you confirm.

I consider myself an OG Black Friday skeptic. Back in 2011, I told the New York Times (gift link) that after crunching the price data at my startup Decide.com, the lowest electronics prices usually came in early December, not on Black Friday.

Don’t trust an AI turkey recipe on its own. Back in 2022, when the New York Times cooked a Thanksgiving from GPT-3 recipes, the turkey recipe called for one garlic clove for a 12-pound bird and no butter or oil. It came out dry and flavorless.

Don’t take a chatbot’s word on an airline’s rules. Air Canada’s chatbot told a grieving passenger he could claim a bereavement discount after he flew. The real policy said no, and he had to take the airline to a tribunal to collect $812 (Canadian). Check the airline’s own policy page, and screenshot what the bot tells you.

Don’t click on the deal of the century. Scammers now use AI to make fake shopping sites look legitimate, and the number of fake sites jumped 250% last holiday season, according to NordVPN. Type the retailer’s address yourself.

Don’t try to win the family argument with AI-fetched facts. Even the creator of Angry Uncle Bot says that bombarding your uncle with facts only makes him angrier. Ask questions and listen instead.

Here’s another option: give technology a rest.

Unplug from your devices and from AI, and have an AI-free, 100% human Thanksgiving.

Choose from 60+ sessions across topics and skill levels, from introductory overviews to advanced deep dives. Catch every major launch as it is announced. Customers share what they learned, and select sessions include live Q&A. Livestream registration is free.

#5331. Hackers breach Air Force cloud: 7 things 2026's government hacks exposed, and what to do

From Social Security numbers to FBI agents' home addresses, here's what 2026's government hacks exposed and how to protect yourself

In September, a criminal hacking group called ShinyHunters claimed it had taken data on nearly every FBI agent and job applicant, and knocked the bureau's jobs portal offline. "We have compromised the FBI. We hold very sensitive data on almost ALL FBI Agents and individuals who filed an application with the FBI for a job," the group's message said, according to PBS News. The FBI said it was investigating the claim, but that it hadn't yet determined the "point of breach."

The stakes go beyond identity theft. A New York Times analysis found that the stolen data may include home addresses, Social Security numbers and job assignments. Reuters reported that the hackers claimed to have 2 to 3 terabytes of data, and some of what it reviewed showed which agents work in specific field offices and in units handling intelligence and counterespionage.

In November, the FBI began investigating an apparent hack of the National Crime Information Center, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press. Local, state and federal police use the database to look up fugitives, missing persons, criminal histories and stolen property. The FBI declined to comment, and the scope of the problem wasn't immediately clear.

This exposure reaches people who never worked for the government: anyone named in a police record. "We just heard about it, and I will say that it's not good," President Donald Trump said in a Fox News Channel interview. Administration officials have blamed a separate run of recent outages on routine system upgrades, and there was no immediate sign the two were linked.

The exposures this year haven't been limited to federal agencies. Before the FBI's jobs portal was hit, a separate breach may have exposed more than 153 million driver's licenses across the U.S. and Canada, TIME reports. Sherman's warning about not dismissing "just another data breach" was written about that leak.

Combined with Social Security numbers and job details from other breaches, a license record helps a scammer build a fuller profile of one person.

Each breach adds a piece; together they can complete the picture.

Government hacks tend to be covered as stories about secrets and spies. The breaches that have piled up through 2026 are mostly about something closer to home: the personal records of the people who serve, work for or deal with federal agencies. Social Security numbers, home addresses, job assignments and criminal records have all been in the path of intruders this year.

"It can be tempting to dismiss the next hack of a database as 'just another data breach.'... But breaches do not exist in a vacuum," Justin Sherman, a senior associate at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, wrote, as TIME reported. Each exposed record can make the next scam or intrusion easier. Here's what has been exposed so far, and what people caught up in it can do.

The largest confirmed exposure this year came from the Defense Manpower Data Center, the Pentagon office that keeps personnel records for pay, healthcare and retirement. A Pentagon official confirmed to TIME that about 2.76 million living people and 294,000 deceased people were affected. The exposed files included Social Security numbers and job details, along with names, birthdates and contact information.

The center holds records on more than 60 million people, including troops, civilian staff, contractors, family members, retirees and veterans. So the breach reached well beyond people currently in uniform. Intruders had access to a file-sharing server from October 2025 until the center found the weakness on July 16, 2026. Notification letters went out in September, and it's still unclear which files were opened or who did it.

For anyone linked to the military, the most sensitive number they have may already be in someone else's hands.

ShinyHunters says this attack wasn't about money. It gave the FBI one week to retract a May public advisory that called the group a "cyber criminal group specializing in large-scale data breaches and extortion," and said it was "offended" by the description. "This is not a ransom, coercion, or extortion. Your federal policies do not apply here. This PSA is NOT financially motivated," the message said.

The FBI's own advisory had warned that the group often uses "real or exaggerated claims of access" to pressure victims. That means its claims about how much it took can't be taken at face value. The group didn't say what it would do if the deadline passed.

Whether the motive is money or pride, the data is the same once it's out.

A breach here would put ordinary Americans' records at risk, not just federal staff's.

The FBI's troubles started earlier in the year. In March, the bureau said it was investigating "suspicious activities" on an internal system holding sensitive information about surveillance operations and investigations. That same month, a pro-Iranian hacking group claimed to have hacked an account belonging to FBI Director Kash Patel and posted what appeared to be old photos, a resume and personal documents more than a decade old.

The FBI said the Patel material was "historical in nature" and involved "no government information." Together, the incidents show how often the bureau itself has become a target this year.

Even old personal documents give attackers something to work with.

The Pentagon is offering a year of free credit monitoring and identity-restoration services through IDX, a private firm it hired. People with questions can contact IDX at response.idx.us/DMDC or 1-855-744-4556, a defense official told TIME.

Anyone can also place a free credit freeze with each of the three major credit bureaus (Equifax, Experian and TransUnion), according to the Federal Trade Commission. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in a person's name. Active-duty troops and National Guard members can also get free electronic credit monitoring. Experts also warn that exposed records make phishing easier, so unexpected messages that cite personal details deserve extra suspicion.

A credit freeze costs nothing and takes minutes, and it's the simplest protection after a breach.

#5330. Should You Run Your Own AI or Pay a Provider? Here’s How to Decide.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Open-weight models finally give businesses a real choice between running AI on their own servers or renting it from the cloud.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

I’m an AI engineer and I’m currently building ChatMakr, an AI-powered platform that creates multi-agent chatbots in seconds, powered by open-weight models. I also spent time at a consulting firm focused on innovation financing, where I talked with hundreds of Parisian entrepreneurs, and this exact question — run it yourself or rent it from someone else — came up constantly. Open-weight models have made that question sharper than ever, so here’s how to actually think through it.

An open-weight model is a model whose trained parameters are published for anyone to download and run, without necessarily sharing the code or data used to train it. As the Open Source Initiative defines it, “Open Weights refer to the final weights and biases of a trained neural network.” You get the finished brain, not the recipe that built it. That distinction is exactly why open-weight models matter for this decision: because you can download the weights, you’re free to run them on your own hardware, on a cloud provider’s hardware or switch between the two, instead of being locked into one company’s API.

Self-hosting means running that open-weight model on infrastructure you control, whether that’s a GPU server sitting in your own office or a rented GPU virtual machine you fully manage. You pick the hardware, you install the software and you’re responsible for keeping it running.

Cloud means renting inference from a provider instead, whether that’s a managed endpoint hosting an open-weight model for you or a closed API you call over the internet. But cloud isn’t one single choice, because where that provider is headquartered changes what legal system governs your data. A U.S. cloud provider, even one running a data center inside the EU, remains bound by the CLOUD Act.

Here’s how it actually plays out. Below, I’ll call the winner between self-host and cloud on six specific fronts.

Self-hosting looks expensive on paper because you’re paying for a GPU whether you use it or not, but at high enough volume that fixed cost stops mattering. Cloudzy’s cost analysis explains that “self-hosting an open-weight model on a GPU VPS can beat a frontier API at high, sustained volume with good GPU utilization.” The catch is that most businesses never generate that kind of steady, maxed-out traffic. For anyone below that threshold, cloud wins on cost.

Running your own GPUs doesn’t just cost hardware money, it costs people, and that line item is easy to underestimate. Activepieces breaks down the real total cost of ownership and finds that “the payroll for these positions often exceeds the annual budget for the H100 GPUs they manage.” The engineers who keep a self-hosted stack alive frequently cost more than the chips they’re maintaining. Cloud wins here, because the provider absorbs that staffing burden for you.

For businesses handling sensitive or regulated data, who can legally compel access to your information matters as much as who can technically breach it. MassiveGRID lays out the jurisdiction problem plainly: “a U.S.-headquartered provider operating servers in the EU is still subject to the CLOUD Act,” while “a provider incorporated and operating entirely within the EU provides stronger protection against extraterritorial data access requests.” Self-hosting on your own hardware or choosing an EU-only cloud provider closes off that exposure entirely. Self-hosting, or EU cloud specifically, wins on legal exposure.

Demand for AI products rarely arrives in a straight line, and that’s where renting infrastructure pays off. Buzzclan defines the core benefit of cloud elasticity as “the ability to automatically adjust infrastructure capacity based on demand, helping businesses maintain performance without overprovisioning.” A self-hosted GPU server can’t grow on demand during a traffic spike or shrink back down when things go quiet, it just sits at whatever size you bought it at. Cloud wins on scalability.

Open-weight models exist precisely because businesses want to shape the model itself, not just prompt around its limits. A closed cloud API gives you a fixed model behind a fixed interface. Self-hosting wins on customization.

For a business selling into enterprise customers, a provider’s paperwork can matter as much as its performance. Google Cloud explains what its SOC 2 report actually verifies: “the SOC 2 reports are generated by an objective third party attesting to a set of assertions made by Google Cloud about its controls that are in place to protect customer data.” Building that same audited trail yourself, on your own servers, takes real time and specialized staff most startups don’t have. Cloud wins on compliance.

There’s no single winner here, and that’s the actual takeaway. Open-weight models made this a genuine choice instead of a forced one: The same model can run in a rented data center or on a box you own, and the right answer depends on which of these six factors matters most to your business right now.

If you’re regulated or handling sensitive data, lean self-host or EU cloud. If you’re scaling unpredictably or don’t want to hire an infrastructure team, lean cloud. Most businesses will end up doing both — cloud for the unpredictable parts, self-hosting for the parts that need full control — and that’s not indecision; it’s just matching the infrastructure to the actual argument that matters most in each case.

I’m an AI engineer and I’m currently building ChatMakr, an AI-powered platform that creates multi-agent chatbots in seconds, powered by open-weight models. I also spent time at a consulting firm focused on innovation financing, where I talked with hundreds of Parisian entrepreneurs, and this exact question — run it yourself or rent it from someone else — came up constantly. Open-weight models have made that question sharper than ever, so here’s how to actually think through it.

An open-weight model is a model whose trained parameters are published for anyone to download and run, without necessarily sharing the code or data used to train it. As the Open Source Initiative defines it, “Open Weights refer to the final weights and biases of a trained neural network.” You get the finished brain, not the recipe that built it. That distinction is exactly why open-weight models matter for this decision: because you can download the weights, you’re free to run them on your own hardware, on a cloud provider’s hardware or switch between the two, instead of being locked into one company’s API.

Self-hosting means running that open-weight model on infrastructure you control, whether that’s a GPU server sitting in your own office or a rented GPU virtual machine you fully manage. You pick the hardware, you install the software and you’re responsible for keeping it running.

#5329. Inflation is squeezing Americans so hard that rising grocery bills are now a top reason Black Friday shoppers are cutting back

Black Friday has arrived, and the National Retail Federation expects about 126 million Americans to shop today, part of an estimated 182.7 million who plan to shop over the Thanksgiving holiday weekend.

But many of those shoppers are heading out with less to spend, with the cost of groceries being a main reason why. Among Black Friday shoppers who are cutting back this year, 68% point to rising grocery costs, up from 57% in 2025, according to a new survey from market research firm Drive Research. Rising living costs are still the top reason, cited by 76%, up from 70%, while 61% blame inflation, up from 54%.

Black Friday budgets are shrinking as a result. Some 41% of Black Friday shoppers expect to spend less on holiday shopping than they did last year, up from 31% in 2025. The share who typically spend $1,000 or more fell to 18% from 24%, and 34% said they feel pressured to spend more on gifts than they can comfortably afford.

Everyday essentials are also on shopping lists. Household necessities like groceries and cleaning supplies are among the planned purchases for 38% of in-person Black Friday shoppers and 31% of those shopping online. Drive Research surveyed 1,405 U.S. adults from Oct. 6 to Oct. 9, and its Black Friday findings are based on the 1,025 respondents who plan to shop over the weekend.

Grocery prices rose 0.4% in October, the biggest monthly increase since April, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, with beef up 0.9%. Over the 12 months through September, food-at-home prices climbed 1.8%, while overall consumer prices rose 3.7%. Gas has driven much of that broader increase: gasoline prices were up 37.4% from a year earlier in October, before seasonal adjustment. The BLS couldn’t publish most year-over-year comparisons for October because it didn’t collect price data in October 2025 during the government shutdown.

Federal Reserve officials have taken notice. Michelle Bowman, the Fed’s vice chair for supervision, said in a Nov. 10 speech the labor market had improved more than she expected this year, but that “our progress on lowering inflation has disappointed.” The Fed held its benchmark rate in a range of 3.75% to 4% at its October meeting.

Walmart remains the top in-store Black Friday destination, with 71% of in-person shoppers planning a visit—the same share for the third straight year—according to Drive Research. Emily Rodgers, the company’s director of marketing, said when budgets are tight, “shoppers stick with the stores they already trust to have low prices.”

Walmart CEO John Furner said last week rising diesel and transportation costs have added about $2 billion in expenses this year, which could make it harder to keep prices low through the holidays.

“We will do everything we can in terms of efficiency,” Furner said on the company’s post-earnings call.

Shoppers also aren’t sure the deals are real. Some 64% of Black Friday shoppers believe retailers raise prices ahead of the sales so the discounts aren’t genuine, and 72% said the deals aren’t nearly as good as they used to be, Drive Research found.

“Black Friday used to sell itself on the date alone. Now shoppers show up with a price tracker in one hand and a healthy dose of doubt in the other,” Rodgers said. “The retailers who win will be the ones who show their math: what the item sold for last month and what the customer actually saves today.”

Most consumers are trying to hold the line. Some 82% are taking steps to manage holiday costs, including buying less expensive gifts (25%), cutting back in other areas (24%) and buying for fewer people (20%), according to NRF’s survey of 7,956 adults.

A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on Nov. 5, 2025.

Sydney Lake is an associate editor at Fortune, where she writes and edits news for the publication's global news desk.

#5328. FCC clears SpaceX to put up to a million satellites in orbit for Starmind data center network

by Alan Boyle on Nov 25, 2026 at 4:46 pmNovember 25, 2026 at 4:46 pm

The Federal Communications Commission has authorized SpaceX to send up to a million satellites into orbit for its Starmind data-processing network.

In a news release, the FCC touted today’s decision as “the first authorization in U.S. history for a constellation of data centers in space” and echoed the high-flown language that SpaceX used to describe the network in its application 10 months ago.

“It promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilization — one that can harness the full power of the sun,” the agency said.

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said the plan “opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.”

Carr signaled that he was all in on the Trump administration’s support for rapid data center expansion, despite a growing backlash that figured in this month’s midterm elections. He said that “compute campuses or data centers are essential to sustaining America’s leadership” in artificial intelligence.

“By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment,” Carr said.

In a post to X, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk told Carr that his praise was “much appreciated.”

“This will be a great asset to America and the world,” Musk said.

Proponents of solar-powered orbital data centers say such constellations will address the top concerns about terrestrial data centers, including land use, power consumption and water requirements for cooling. Critics point to the engineering challenges, including concerns about cooling the satellites, managing space traffic and dealing with orbital debris.

In approving SpaceX’s application, the FCC rejected opposition from Amazon and Viasat, as well as from the American Astronomical Society, which raised concerns about the constellation’s impact on the night sky. The AAS said in a statement that it was “disheartened and dismayed” by the FCC’s decision.

The FCC attached several conditions to its authorization, including requirements for communications backups, regular updates and a detailed plan for orbital debris mitigation.

SpaceX was cleared to operate its satellites at orbits ranging from 500 to 1,002 kilometers (310 to 623 miles) in altitude. The first satellite is to be put into operation no later than 2033, and the FCC calls for the full constellation to be operating by 2040.

In August, SpaceX announced that it was partnering with Nvidia to design the compute payload for the Starmind AI1 satellite. “Each of the Starmind satellites will include Nvidia Rubin GPUs and Vera CPUs for datacenter-class space compute,” SpaceX said at the time.

SpaceX’s facility in Redmond, Wash., makes the satellites for the Starlink telecommunications network — but in a filing related to this year’s initial public offering, SpaceX said its operation in Bastrop, Texas, would be put in charge of producing AI compute satellites.

The FCC said it is continuing to review additional orbital data center proposals and intends to issue decisions on each proposal “according to the agency’s regular procedures.”

#5327. The Simple AI Framework I Use to Cut Administrative Waste

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

AI delivers the greatest business impact when it’s implemented strategically to eliminate repetitive administrative work, reduce burnout and free employees to focus on high-value, relationship-driven tasks.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

When I opened my first physical therapy practice, I believed growth depended on seeing more patients. That mindset worked for a while, until I realized my team and I were spending hours every day on paperwork, scheduling and insurance tasks instead of patient care. Administrative work had quietly become the biggest obstacle to growth.

Years later, after building therapy, staffing and hospice companies, I see artificial intelligence the same way I see any business tool: Its value comes from solving a real operational problem. AI should give your people more time to serve customers and build relationships. Everything else is secondary. That philosophy has shaped how we use technology across our businesses.

Spend a week identifying every repetitive task that eats up valuable time. Look for work that follows the same steps every day and requires little judgment. Those processes usually deliver the fastest return when automated.

In health care, charting, appointment scheduling and insurance verification quickly rose to the top of our list. Every industry has its own version of these tasks. Find them before you buy any technology.

Resist the urge to automate everything at once. Doing so can overwhelm you and your team, and it makes it hard to tell which changes worked and which flopped.

Start with the one to three administrative processes that consume the most hours each week. For us, documentation was the obvious first choice. AI-assisted transcription dramatically reduced the time clinicians spent writing notes, so they could focus on patients instead of keyboards.

We also introduced AI tools for scheduling and insurance verification. Those systems reduced delays and freed employees to handle conversations that required empathy and critical thinking.

Many leaders evaluate AI by asking whether the software costs less than another employee. I prefer a different question: How many productive hours did the technology return to the business?

If documentation falls from 30 minutes to five minutes per appointment, those recovered hours create measurable capacity. Teams can serve more customers, improve quality or simply leave work on time. Revenue often follows, but the first win is reclaimed time.

Tracking time savings also keeps expectations realistic. Every automation project should produce measurable improvements before you expand it to another department.

Every AI project deserves a simple scorecard. Track how many hours employees save each week, how quickly customers get a response, how many errors disappear from the process and how your team feels after the change. Those measurements show whether the technology is delivering real value or just adding another subscription to the budget.

Review these metrics every month. Small improvements often compound into significant operational gains over time. Consistent measurement also helps employees see the purpose behind each new tool, which builds confidence and speeds adoption across the organization.

Burnout rarely begins with meaningful work. It usually begins with repetitive work.

Few health care professionals entered the field because they loved paperwork, and entrepreneurs in every industry can relate. Endless administrative duties drain energy that could go to customers, employees or strategic planning.

When AI removes repetitive work, people get back to the work that inspired them in the first place, and burnout drops as a result. In our businesses, clinicians give more attention to patient conversations because documentation happens in the background. That shift improves both the employee experience and the customer experience.

Successful adoption comes from discipline, not speed. Begin with one department. Select one workflow. Define one success metric. Once that process delivers consistent results, move on to the next opportunity.

This phased approach builds confidence throughout the organization. Employees see practical improvements instead of another technology initiative that creates extra work. Leaders also gain reliable data before making larger investments.

Small wins create momentum that large transformations rarely achieve on day one.

One common misconception is that AI is meant to replace people. It isn’t.

Technology should strengthen human capability, not replace human judgment. Every automation decision we make comes back to the same question: Will this give our people more time for work that requires experience, compassion and creative thinking?

That principle has guided our investments, from AI documentation to administrative automation. Technology handles repetition. People handle relationships. Together, they build stronger businesses than either could alone.

Once we put these changes in place, the difference was almost immediate. Clinicians spent less time on documentation after appointments and more time engaging with patients during them. Front office teams fielded fewer routine calls because scheduling and administrative questions moved through AI-powered workflows, which reduced delays and made the experience smoother for everyone.

What surprised me most was the ripple effect. Employees felt less overwhelmed because they could focus on work that required their expertise. Leaders had better visibility into operations because we were measuring performance instead of reacting to problems. Those improvements gave us the confidence to expand AI into other areas of the business, one process at a time.

The experience reinforced something I’ve believed throughout my career: Sustainable growth comes from building systems that free talented people to do what they do best. AI became one more tool that helped us deliver better care, strengthen our operations and prepare our businesses for the next stage of growth.

When I opened my first physical therapy practice, I believed growth depended on seeing more patients. That mindset worked for a while, until I realized my team and I were spending hours every day on paperwork, scheduling and insurance tasks instead of patient care. Administrative work had quietly become the biggest obstacle to growth.

Years later, after building therapy, staffing and hospice companies, I see artificial intelligence the same way I see any business tool: Its value comes from solving a real operational problem. AI should give your people more time to serve customers and build relationships. Everything else is secondary. That philosophy has shaped how we use technology across our businesses.

Spend a week identifying every repetitive task that eats up valuable time. Look for work that follows the same steps every day and requires little judgment. Those processes usually deliver the fastest return when automated.

#5326. ‘Aether & Iron’: Seattle-area indie game studio builds a noir detective RPG in the sky

by Thomas Wilde on Nov 26, 2026 at 8:51 amNovember 26, 2026 at 8:51 am

Some video games exist at the confluence point between a surprising number of genres, which can make them difficult to explain to people who aren’t hip-deep in the hobby. That’s why several of the most popular categories are currently nicknamed after the most visible games in them, such as the “Metroidvania” or “Soulslike.” Sure, this isn’t anywhere near the biggest problem in the video game industry at the moment, but we’re going to have to figure this out sooner or later.

Aether & Iron, created by the Issaquah, Wash.-based developer Seismic Squirrel, with co-developer Chaos Theory Games, is at one of those weird genre points. It’s described by its developers as a “narrative RPG,” which works well enough, but that also doesn’t exactly say that much.

It’s worth saying up front that Aether & Iron is on a slow boil. It’s a 30-hour game that unfolds at a careful pace, building out an elaborate science-fiction setting from first principles. If you’re looking for fast thrills, it’s not the experience for you. Instead, think of it like a long novel with points of potential failure, where every opportunity for interactivity is also a chance for you to take its story in a different direction.

Aether & Iron is set in an alternate universe where a strange substance called aether was found beneath Manhattan in 1871. Sixty-seven years later, the study and exploitation of aether has become its own branch of science, which led to a great technological leap forward. Much of New York has been transformed into a three-tiered flying city, split between the Lowers, the Uppers and the Heights. The higher a neighborhood flies, the higher its society.

You enter the story in 1938 in the role of Gia Randazzo, a smuggler from the Lowers who’s hit hard times. She’s so desperate for work that she takes a job she shouldn’t, as a driver and bodyguard for a young scientist from the Heights named Eleanor Reinhardt. It should be a milk run, but Dr. Reinhardt has enemies she doesn’t know about.

In short order, an assassin tries to kill them both, someone steals Gia’s car, and she and Dr. Reinhardt end up stuck together in the worst parts of the Lowers. With no money, a loaner vehicle and few friends left, Gia has to figure out who wants Dr. Reinhardt dead and why. That puts her on a collision course with a revolutionary movement, several of New York’s power brokers and a conspiracy that could knock the city back out of the sky.

You could call Aether & Iron something like “airship noir.” Despite its science-fiction trappings, it’s a dark detective novel at heart. Yes, humanity’s built up into the sky, but the street is always the street. Mickey Spillane meets William Gibson.

During dialogue and investigation sequences, Aether & Iron uses a pair of virtual six-sided dice to determine whether you succeed or fail at a given task. As you get further into the game, you can acquire items that let you reroll those dice on a failed check.

More importantly, you earn experience points for accomplishments and victories, which grant you skill points that can be spent in one of nine categories. You can customize Gia to follow several distinct character tracks, such as a detective, a back-alley brawler or a fast-talking con woman. That influences the path you take through the game and the options that become available to you.

No matter how you choose to play Gia, you can’t always avoid a fight. All the combat in Aether & Iron takes place behind the wheel, with Gia and her crew driving customized vehicles. You can acquire a whole fleet of cars and trucks, then kit them out with special weapons, utility devices, armored plates and matching paint jobs.

Each fight consists of a turn-based tactical battle through the streets in and around New York. In addition to simply shooting up an enemy, you can sideswipe them to force them off the road or into other cars.

Many of the city’s thoroughfares are falling apart or prone to sudden lane changes, so most fights will have their own set of additional hazards. Fortunately, they’re as dangerous to your enemies as they are to you, so you can exploit the road hazards if you think fast enough.

If I had to point at one problem I’ve got with Aether & Iron, it might be that the combat has a couple of unlabeled difficulty curves. Specifically, a few fights are built around specific types of damage to such a degree that the only real way past them is to reload an old save and modify all my vehicles for that particular encounter.

If you like the idea of constantly tweaking your vehicle collection for specific combat purposes, like heat shielding or knockback resistance, you’ll have some fun here. If you’re like me and you tend to rely on set-and-forget general-purpose builds, you’ll run into some roadblocks.

Other than that, you might know already whether or not you want to check it out. There’s a lot of care and art in Aether & Iron, mixed with a unique science-fiction setting that isn’t quite like anything else in video games at the moment.

Aether & Iron is currently available for PC and Mac via Steam for $24.99. Seismic Squirrel plans to release the game for PlayStation and Xbox in 2027.

#5325. How To Build Influence Without Waiting for Authority

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Building influence requires more than a leadership title or strong job performance. By developing relationships, gathering evidence, earning trust and taking initiative, professionals can shape decisions, create meaningful change and establish themselves as leaders before receiving formal authority.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Early in my career, I believed excellent work would eventually create its own reward. I became the person people trusted to solve problems, take on difficult assignments and deliver when the stakes were high. Yet there is a trap hidden inside reliability: You can become indispensable to the work without becoming influential in the decisions that determine it.

I eventually learned to separate authority from influence. Authority comes with a title or responsibility for the final decision. Influence is your ability to move an idea, change an outcome or bring people with you regardless of what appears beneath your name in an email signature.

That distinction matters because waiting for authority can consume years. Influence can begin from almost any position, including one far from the executive table.

When I enter an organization as a consultant, I spend the early stretch watching. I want to understand who people consult before making a decision, whose objections carry weight and who has direct access to the person making the final call.

The organizational chart provides useful information, but it rarely shows the full picture. I think of the real structure as a web. To start mapping yours, study a few decisions and ask:

Write down what you observe. Look for patterns rather than focusing only on seniority. This helps you see where your relationships and contributions can have greater impact and where you may have been spending energy with little effect on the final outcome.

I learned this while working to improve outcomes for Black women inside an organization. During my first several months, I created programs, workshops and employee groups. Leadership was pleased, yet I could see that we were addressing individual women while leaving larger cultural problems untouched.

Instead of walking into an executive meeting and declaring that the approach needed to change, I gathered evidence. I examined exit interviews, studied promotion patterns, found allies prepared for deeper change and ran small pilots that demonstrated another approach.

By the time I pushed for a larger change, I had evidence, results and people behind me. Over roughly 18 months, the work became more strategic because I had built the influence required to change how the problem was understood.

Before making your next significant proposal, gather three things:

An idea becomes harder to dismiss when other people can see what you see. Building support early also gives people an opportunity to improve the idea before you bring it into a higher-stakes conversation.

Being excellent at your job creates credibility, but credibility alone can leave you with more assignments rather than greater impact. People know you will deliver, so they keep handing you things to deliver. Eventually, being the dependable person can become its own holding pattern.

Use the trust you have earned to shape the work itself. Propose an improvement, ask to participate earlier in a project or volunteer to lead an initiative that connects you with people outside your immediate team. Keep a record of problems solved, measurable outcomes and moments when colleagues sought your judgment.

Credibility sitting still makes you useful. Credibility applied to decisions expands your influence.

Many professionals concentrate their relationship-building efforts on senior executives. Yet influence rarely travels through a single relationship. Peers, colleagues in other departments, administrative professionals and people closer to customers can all help an idea move.

The Revolutionary Pathmakers I write about have historically created networks through community and cross-functional relationships when conventional pathways were unavailable. Those relationships provided information, support and opportunities that formal structures alone failed to provide.

This is not just history. My research found that Black women who lead from values rather than position build more sustainable authority than traditional power-based models, with higher retention and better long-term results. When the formal channels are closed, influence built through relationships and shared values is not the backup plan. It turns out to be the stronger one.

Identify two people outside your usual circle and learn what they are trying to accomplish. Ask what repeatedly creates difficulty for them and where your work intersects. Enter those conversations looking for ways to contribute rather than immediately asking for something.

Influence grows when people experience your contribution before you need their support.

I often coach people who describe having little power while simultaneously outlining solutions they can put into motion. The question I ask is simple: What can you responsibly begin from where you are?

You might test one part of an idea, improve a recurring process, connect people working separately or gather evidence around a problem nobody owns. Start small enough that the idea can prove itself, then document the result. Pay attention to what worked, who benefited and what would be required to expand it.

A successful experiment gives you something stronger than a proposal about what might work. It gives you evidence of what already did.

I spent years being excellent while being overlooked. What changed my trajectory was understanding that waiting for recognition was delaying the leadership I was already capable of practicing.

Influence grows when you understand how decisions move, build relationships before you need them, use your credibility intentionally and create opportunities to demonstrate what you can do. These actions can begin well before a promotion appears.

There is one more piece, and it may be the one that matters most. Moral clarity. The influence that lasts belongs to people who stand for something bigger than their own advancement. When you are clear about what you are for, and consistent about it, people follow you because of what you represent, not just what you can do for them. Authority can be granted. Moral authority has to be earned, and it is the kind no one can take back.

A title can expand your authority, but your ability to make an impact can begin long before anyone changes the words beneath your name. The question is whether you will wait for that change or start using the influence you already have.

Early in my career, I believed excellent work would eventually create its own reward. I became the person people trusted to solve problems, take on difficult assignments and deliver when the stakes were high. Yet there is a trap hidden inside reliability: You can become indispensable to the work without becoming influential in the decisions that determine it.

I eventually learned to separate authority from influence. Authority comes with a title or responsibility for the final decision. Influence is your ability to move an idea, change an outcome or bring people with you regardless of what appears beneath your name in an email signature.

That distinction matters because waiting for authority can consume years. Influence can begin from almost any position, including one far from the executive table.

#5324. What’s Next For Recruiting, Job Hunting And HR? More AI, Of Course

AI agents and humanoid robots may dominate the funding headlines. But even so, investors haven’t lost interest in startups focused on finding, filling and managing jobs for actual humans.

So far this year, venture backers have poured close to $4 billion into an assortment of global companies focused on recruiting, finding jobs and streamlining processes associated with HR and payroll management, Crunchbase data shows. Not surprisingly, the vast majority are also incorporating a heavy dose of AI.

To get a sense where capital is flowing, we used Crunchbase data to analyze investment to employment-related categories for the past few years. Broadly, findings show 2026 funding on track to meet or slightly exceed year-ago levels, albeit with reduced deal count.

Much of this year’s investment has gone to a small group of companies. To illustrate, below we put together a list of 14 of the largest fundraisers.

As you can see, it’s a varied list, with a commonly shared theme of bringing more automation to hiring, HR and payroll tasks.

By far the largest funding recipient is Mercor, a startup that pairs human experts with developers of AI models and tools. The 4-year-old company raised $750 million in a Series D round this month at a whopping $20 billion valuation.

San Francisco-based Mercor is betting that as companies build AI agents to take on more work tasks, demand for subject matter experts to guide these efforts will grow. While frontier labs have been its primary buyers for the past few years, Mercor says it expects enterprises will soon be its major customers.

The next two largest fundraisers on our list for this year are focused on automating more employer tasks. Paris-based Skello secured $220 million this summer for its AI-enabled software platform for HR teams. And HiBob, a New York-based platform for HR and payroll, picked up $166 million in a Salesforce1-led financing.

Of course, investors aren’t only looking at startups automating work tasks or training AI agents to do so. They’re also backing companies focused on the old-fashioned business of matching workers and employers.

In this sector, one of the larger rounds this year went to San Francisco-based Juicebox, an AI tool for recruiters to find talented candidates. The 4-year-old company picked up an $80 million Series B at an $850 million valuation.

Agentic hiring is also a thing. Metaview, a San Francisco-based startup that offers an agentic recruiting platform optimized, in its words, to “get the right butts in seats,” secured $60 million in a September Series C financing. Around the same time, London’s Jack & Jill AI, which offers AI agents for finding careers and for hiring, closed on $40 million in Series A funding.

Another agentic hiring platform, San Francisco’s Paraform, announced a $40 million round this spring, pitching itself as an offering for an age in which employers are making fewer hires overall but still need highly skilled people for highly paid jobs.

So what kind of employment future do startup funding trends paint for human jobseekers?

Not a good one. As a human who has spent decades writing about sector-specific startup funding, this is probably the most depressing data dive into investment trends for an industry that I have ever done.

Overall, the bulk of big rounds are going to one of three categories: using humans to help train their potential AI replacements, automating work tasks around supporting people in the workplace, and getting AI to help hire the right people for the dwindling pool of available positions.

Typically, I’m rooting for startups to succeed. And honestly, there’s not an individual company highlighted here that I’m specifically hoping will fail. But nonetheless, the broad vision of an increasingly AI-dominated workplace does bring with it a sense of trepidation.

#5323. XRP News: Thanksgiving Rally or December 1 Supply Shock?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

XRP has a history of making Thanksgiving interesting, old news for some. In 2024, Ripple surged nearly 49% in the three days following the holiday. Last year, it went nowhere. Now, XRP is heading into another Thanksgiving with $1 in sight and Ripple’s 1 billion-token escrow unlock looming on December 1.

The timing puts bulls in a tight spot. XRP is recovering from a November sell-off, but the rebound has yet to clear major resistance. A holiday rally could give buyers some breathing room before next week’s token release puts supply back in the spotlight.

The 2024 Thanksgiving weekend was anything but quiet for XRP. The token closed November 28 at $1.54, climbed to $1.80 the following day, and reached $2.29 by December 1. That was a gain of nearly 49% from Thanksgiving’s close.

The rally had fuel beyond holiday trading as Donald Trump’s election victory revived hopes for a friendlier crypto regulatory environment, while XRP was breaking out after years of being held back by its SEC lawsuit. Buyers were chasing momentum, and the long weekend did little to slow them down.

Last year’s price action was considerably less exciting. XRP closed Thanksgiving on November 27, 2025, near $2.20, then drifted around $2.16 over the following days. The market offered no repeat of the explosive move seen a year earlier.

That history makes this year’s comparison interesting, but the conditions are different. XRP is entering Thanksgiving after a painful November decline.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

XRP’s recovery toward $0.95 has brought the psychological $1 level back into play. Buyers have been defending the area below $0.90, preventing another immediate breakdown and giving the short-term chart some breathing room.

But the problem is overhead resistance, as XRP must first push through $0.96–$0.98 before $1 becomes a realistic breakout target. That zone has become the immediate test for buyers. A clean move through it could attract momentum traders and open the path toward $1.02 and $1.08.

The $1 mark matters because XRP has spent November losing ground. Reclaiming it would put the token back above an important psychological threshold and give bulls something concrete to work with.

Failure to break resistance could leave the rebound looking like another dead-cat bounce. XRP’s recent low around $0.89 remains the level to watch. Losing it would put $0.86 back on the radar and risk undoing the recovery.

For now, the chart is caught between an improving short-term bounce and a damaged larger trend. Bulls have a chance, but they need to turn that chance into a breakout.

The next complication arrives Monday, with Ripple’s scheduled escrow contracts. It will release 1 billion XRP, renewing concerns about supply just as the token tries to recover from bad geopolitical news.

The billion-token headline sounds worse than Ripple’s typical net release. Over the past year, the company has re-escrowed around 70% of monthly unlocks, leaving around 300 million XRP outside escrow on average. The market will be watching whether December follows the same pattern.

The full 1 billion XRP unlock is not equivalent to 1 billion tokens hitting exchanges for sale. What Ripple re-locks, retains, or moves afterward will determine how much circulating supply actually changes.

What does it need? XRP cannot afford to enter Monday with a failed breakout and weakening support. If buyers reclaim $1 before the unlock, sentiment could shift in their favor. If XRP remains pinned below resistance, the escrow event gives nervous traders another reason to stay cautious.

Thanksgiving delivered XRP a spectacular rally in 2024. This year, bulls need more than a holiday repeat; they need the $1 back.

#5322. Startup Spotlight: Aventide builds AI client management software for consultants and coaches

Startup Spotlight profiles tech startups in the Pacific Northwest.

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 27, 2026 at 7:30 amNovember 25, 2026 at 2:33 pm

Christian Quiver and Eric Baxter met in a grocery store parking lot, introduced by their wives. Quiver needed a designer for a project, so the two swapped numbers and agreed to try working together for 90 days. Four years later, they’re building a startup together in the Columbia River Gorge.

Their startup, Aventide, opened to the public on Oct. 29. It’s AI-powered software for consultants, coaches and others who sell their expertise one client at a time. Aventide drafts proposals, invoices and follow-ups, but nothing goes to a client until the owner approves it.

Eric Baxter, CDO, and Christian Quiver, CEO, Founder

The name blends “abhainn,” the Irish Gaelic word for river, with “tide,” for the spot where a river meets the sea and where towns and ports have long grown up.

Quiver, the CEO, lives in White Salmon, Wash., and spent more than five years at Amazon. He led go-to-market for the in-store experience as Amazon’s device stores grew from two locations to 50. Baxter is chief design officer and lives in nearby Trout Lake. He spent 25 years in product design, including nearly seven years leading user experience at Welocalize, whose clients included Amazon, Google and Apple.

The idea started in 2025 with a question from Baxter’s wife: Which part of his decades of designing products for other people actually brought him joy? His answer was helping people, especially those pushed out by AI-era layoffs who were trying to start something of their own. Quiver bought in that October.

The pair spent more than six months testing with three groups of business owners in the Gorge, including at a demo day in June with the Mid-Columbia Innovation Hub. They kept meeting people who live in small towns and sell their expertise to companies in Seattle or Portland. “A consultant in a small town can land a corporate client,” Quiver said in an email.

The two-person company is bootstrapped and says 81 people are using Aventide so far. After a 14-day free trial, plans cost $39 or $99 a month. Aventide also publishes estimates of the electricity and water behind everyday tasks in the app. Quiver says the figures could be off by a factor of two either way. “If you ask what it costs in electricity and water to use our product, you get a straight answer,” he said.

We caught up with Quiver for this edition of GeekWire’s Startup Spotlight.

In 50 words or less, give us your startup’s elevator pitch?

Aventide is an AI-native client management platform for people paid by the session, project or event. It replaces separate booking, proposal, contract, portal and invoice apps, and runs more than one business from one login.

What problem are you obsessed with solving?

Tool fragmentation in small client businesses, and the fact that the owner ends up being the human glue holding all of it together.

What surprised you after talking to customers?

That the barrier isn’t price or features. People don’t have time to switch systems, and many aren’t comfortable with their own software stack. So we onboard anyone who wants it one-on-one.

How has AI changed the way you build your company?

Everything. It has fundamentally changed what a small team can build and run. We have always worked as experience builders first, and AI lets a team of two think bigger, test faster, and deliver a world-class product that would have taken what seems like 100-200 people just a year or two ago. It cuts our time from idea to execution by at least 50x.

What’s one thing people misunderstand about your startup?

People hear “AI for small business” and picture a chat box taped onto legacy software. Instead of making you click through old CRM menus with a writing bot on the side, Aventide wires AI directly into your bookings, contracts, portals, and payments so you just say it, review it and approve.

What’s the toughest decision you’ve made in the past year?

Choosing which problem we wanted to solve. Our original mission was far too vague to build. We set out to help people through the AI era, but the interviews and prototypes kept landing on client services. Following that meant narrowing a big mission into one product for one kind of owner.

What’s the one piece of advice you give to other entrepreneurs?

Think bigger, and focus on the whole experience you want to create. Outside of a few rare cases, narrow single-purpose tools are old hat now because nobody wants another tab to manage. The future belongs to software where someone can say, “This is my one tool for this category of my life.

50,000 human-scale businesses use Aventide to own their client relationships directly, keeping more money in small businesses and giving more time back to the people running them.

#5321. Your Career Is Probably Ignoring Your Strongest Leadership Training: Community

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Community involvement can be a powerful source of leadership skills, professional connections and career opportunities. By recognizing the value of their community experiences, building genuine relationships and making clear requests for support, professionals can turn existing connections into lasting career growth and influence.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

For years, one of the communities shaping my leadership was one I barely counted as professional development: my church. I coordinated programs, worked with volunteers, managed limited resources and built agreement among people with different opinions. Somehow, I still placed those experiences in a separate category from my career.

That separation caused me to overlook something valuable. The places where we live, worship, volunteer, parent and serve can develop serious leadership capabilities while connecting us with people who know how we show up over time. My research has found that Black women with active community relationships can gain professional opportunities through those relationships while developing skills that translate directly into their careers.

The opportunity is bigger than having a large contact list. Professional power grows when you recognize the value already present in your community and learn how to carry it into other parts of your life.

Church taught me things about leadership that no corporate workshop could replicate. Try coordinating people who volunteer their time, have strong opinions and can leave whenever they want. You quickly learn how to communicate, build agreement and keep people moving when a title gives you very little leverage.

I see similar experiences when I work with clients. A mother may sit on several school committees. Someone else coaches youth sports, organizes neighborhood events or leads a sorority chapter. Because these responsibilities happen outside an employer, people frequently discount them.

I offer a simple exercise for changing that perspective. Draw two columns on a piece of paper. On the left, write every meaningful community role you have held. On the right, translate what each role actually required.

The work stays exactly the same. What changes is your ability to recognize and describe its professional value.

My research surfaced another finding that deserves attention. Women carrying significant family and community responsibilities often received professional leads and opportunities through those relationships. Someone they knew from a community group, board, school or family connection thought of them when an opportunity emerged.

This matters because some of the best opportunities begin through conversation before they reach a public job posting. When people have spent time with you in a community setting, they may already know how you handle responsibility, communicate through disagreement or follow through on commitments.

Take inventory of the communities you already participate in and ask:

The goal is greater than finding someone who can get you a job. It is allowing people who already know your character and capabilities to understand the fuller range of what you can contribute.

A quick word on friend raising, which is my name for building genuine, reciprocal relationships instead of collecting contacts. I have written about it at length elsewhere, so I will not repeat it here, except to make one point that matters for conversion. The relationship is the raw material. It is not the finished product.

Someone who has watched you contribute for five years knows something about you that a person who exchanged business cards with you five minutes ago never will. That depth is what makes the translation believable when you finally claim it. But building the relationship and converting it into professional power are two different moves, and most people stop after the first.

Strong relationships can create opportunity, but people still need to know what you need. I see professionals build wonderful communities and then struggle to make the second move. They hope someone will somehow infer that they are exploring a board position, looking for clients or considering a career change.

Be direct. You might tell someone, “I’m interested in serving on a nonprofit board where my experience in organizational change would be useful. If you hear of an organization looking for that background, I’d appreciate you keeping me in mind.”

Then give the other person a graceful way to decline. They may lack the right connection, have limited influence in their organization or simply be unable to help at that moment. A healthy relationship should remain whole regardless of the answer.

Community becomes powerful because relationships exist beyond a single exchange. That means your behavior after an ask matters as much as your behavior before it.

If the first time someone hears from you in years is when you need a favor, you are drawing on a relationship you stopped maintaining. Instead, make reciprocity a regular practice. Check in without an agenda. Celebrate other people’s accomplishments. Offer help when you have something useful to contribute, and continue showing up after someone has helped you.

I once thought my church leadership belonged in one box and my professional leadership belonged in another. Today, I see how artificial that separation was. The skills I practiced in the community were part of the same leadership I carried into organizations, consulting engagements and other areas of my life.

Your community may be a church, school, neighborhood group, cultural organization, alumni association or circle of parents you see every week. Look again at the people and experiences you have been treating as separate from your career. You may discover that some of your strongest professional assets have been developing there for years.

Knowing many people gives you contacts. Building reciprocal relationships, recognizing the leadership they develop and learning how to connect those relationships across your life gives you something far more durable: a community that grows stronger as its members create opportunities for one another.

For years, one of the communities shaping my leadership was one I barely counted as professional development: my church. I coordinated programs, worked with volunteers, managed limited resources and built agreement among people with different opinions. Somehow, I still placed those experiences in a separate category from my career.

That separation caused me to overlook something valuable. The places where we live, worship, volunteer, parent and serve can develop serious leadership capabilities while connecting us with people who know how we show up over time. My research has found that Black women with active community relationships can gain professional opportunities through those relationships while developing skills that translate directly into their careers.

The opportunity is bigger than having a large contact list. Professional power grows when you recognize the value already present in your community and learn how to carry it into other parts of your life.
